course.title: The Web: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
course.description: How a page reaches the browser, how HTML and CSS shape it, and how JavaScript brings it to life, read closely enough to predict what the code does before you run it.
course.audience: A capable adult who uses the web every day and has seen some code. They know what a variable and a loop are from cs-basics, and need no previous HTML, CSS or JavaScript.

paragraphs: A web page is delivered as text, and the page on your screen is something the browser builds from that text by fixed rules. It asks a server for the document by its address, reads the HTML in the reply into a tree of elements, matches CSS rules against each element to decide how large it is and where it sits, and then runs the JavaScript, which can change the tree for as long as the page stays open. Because each of those steps follows rules that are written down exactly, much of what a page does can be worked out from its code.

A good deal of what looks arbitrary in web development follows from those rules. A style that seems to be ignored has lost to another rule under a fixed ranking, the expression "5" + 3 gives "53" because JavaScript joins the two as text when one side is a string, and a handler on a parent element that runs when you click its child is following the path an event takes through the tree. Each of these has an answer that can be reached by reading the code carefully, and once you know the rule you can say what a page will do before you open it, and which line is at fault when it does something else.
outcomes: You'll be able to trace a URL to the tree the browser builds.
You'll be able to predict which CSS rule wins and how wide an element will be.
You'll be able to predict what JavaScript prints, including coercion, closures and event-loop order.
You'll be able to read fetch, storage and event code and spot the usual bugs and injection risks.
introduction.prerequisites: You should know what a variable, a condition and a loop are, as in How Computers Solve Problems. No HTML, CSS or JavaScript is assumed.

modules.title: Documents and style
modules.description: How a page reaches the browser, how HTML gives it structure, and how CSS decides what every element looks like and where it sits.

modules.title: JavaScript, the language
modules.description: Values, coercion, functions, scope, objects and the event loop, read and traced without a runner.

modules.title: The page comes alive
modules.description: The DOM, events, talking to servers, storing data in the browser, and keeping pages accessible and fast.

concepts.title: Parts of a URL
concepts.summary: A URL names a scheme, a host, an optional port, a path, a query and a fragment, and the browser never sends the fragment to the server.

concepts.title: Request and response
concepts.summary: The browser sends a method, a path and headers, and the server replies with a status code, headers and a body.

concepts.title: Status code families
concepts.summary: The first digit tells the story: 2 means success, 3 redirection, 4 a fault in the request and 5 a fault in the server.

concepts.title: The DOM tree
concepts.summary: The parser turns the HTML text into a tree of nodes, repairing malformed markup by fixed rules instead of failing.

concepts.title: Semantic element
concepts.summary: An element whose name states its role, such as nav, main, button or h2, so that software can use the page without seeing it.

concepts.title: Accessible name
concepts.summary: The text that assistive technology announces for a control, taken from its label, content or alt text.

concepts.title: Heading outline
concepts.summary: Headings h1 to h6 form an outline that readers and screen readers jump through, so levels should follow the content's real nesting.

concepts.title: Label and control
concepts.summary: A label tied to its input by for and id makes the label text part of the control's name and enlarges the click target.

concepts.title: Box model
concepts.summary: Every element is a rectangle of content surrounded by padding, then border, then margin.

concepts.title: box-sizing
concepts.summary: With content-box the declared width covers only the content; with border-box it covers content, padding and border.

concepts.title: Normal flow
concepts.summary: Block boxes stack vertically and inline boxes fill lines, until a layout mode changes that.

concepts.title: Margin collapse
concepts.summary: Adjoining vertical margins between block siblings combine into the larger of the two, not the sum.

concepts.title: Specificity
concepts.summary: A selector's weight is a triple of counts: ids, then classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, then element names and pseudo-elements, compared left to right.

concepts.title: Cascade order
concepts.summary: When specificity ties, the declaration that comes later wins, and !important or inline styles change the ranking.

concepts.title: Inheritance
concepts.summary: Some properties, such as colour and font-family, pass to children unless overridden, while others, such as border and margin, do not.

concepts.title: Custom properties
concepts.summary: A --name value is inherited and read with var(), so one change can restyle many rules.

concepts.title: Flex main axis
concepts.summary: A flex container lays its items along one axis and distributes free space or overflow between them by grow and shrink factors.

concepts.title: Grow and shrink
concepts.summary: Free space is split in proportion to flex-grow and overflow is removed in proportion to flex-shrink times basis.

concepts.title: Grid tracks
concepts.summary: A grid defines rows and columns, and fr units share the space left after fixed tracks and gaps.

concepts.title: Flexbox or grid
concepts.summary: Flexbox arranges one dimension of content-sized items, while grid places items in two dimensions against a track plan.

concepts.title: Relative units
concepts.summary: rem scales from the root font size, em from the element's own or parent's font size, and vw from the viewport width.

concepts.title: Media query
concepts.summary: A media query applies its rules only while its condition, such as min-width, is true for the current viewport.

concepts.title: Mobile first
concepts.summary: Base rules serve the narrowest screen, and min-width queries add complexity as space allows.

concepts.title: Viewport meta
concepts.summary: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers lay the page out at a wide virtual width and shrink it to fit.

concepts.title: Primitive types
concepts.summary: JavaScript has seven primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) and everything else is an object.

concepts.title: Coercion
concepts.summary: Operators convert operands to the type they need: + concatenates if either side is a string, while - * and / convert both sides to numbers.

concepts.title: Strict versus loose equality
concepts.summary: === compares type and value with no conversion, while == converts before comparing, with null == undefined as a special case.

concepts.title: Floating-point numbers
concepts.summary: Numbers are 64-bit floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 and integers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1.

concepts.title: Lexical scope
concepts.summary: A name is resolved by looking outward from where the code was written, not where it is called.

concepts.title: Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
concepts.summary: A function declaration is usable before its line, a var is declared early but undefined until assigned, and let or const throw until their line runs.

concepts.title: Closure
concepts.summary: A function keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in, even after that scope has returned.

concepts.title: Per-iteration binding
concepts.summary: A let in a for loop head creates a fresh binding each iteration, while var shares one across the loop.

concepts.title: References
concepts.summary: Assigning an object or array copies the reference, so two names then point at one object.

concepts.title: Shallow copy
concepts.summary: Spread and Object.assign copy the top level only, so nested objects stay shared.

concepts.title: map, filter and reduce
concepts.summary: map returns a new array of the same length, filter a subset, and reduce folds the array into one value.

concepts.title: Mutating methods
concepts.summary: push, splice and sort change the array in place, while slice, map, filter and toSorted return new ones.

concepts.title: Call stack
concepts.summary: JavaScript runs one piece of synchronous code to completion before anything else runs.

concepts.title: Task and microtask queues
concepts.summary: After the stack empties, all queued microtasks (promise callbacks) run before the next timer or I/O task.

concepts.title: Promise states
concepts.summary: A promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected exactly once, and then callbacks are queued as microtasks.

concepts.title: await
concepts.summary: await pauses the async function and resumes it as a microtask when the awaited promise settles.

concepts.title: DOM API
concepts.summary: The document is a tree of nodes with methods to find, create, change and remove them.

concepts.title: Elements versus nodes
concepts.summary: childNodes includes text and comment nodes, while children includes only elements.

concepts.title: Bubbling and capture
concepts.summary: An event travels down to its target and then back up, firing listeners on each ancestor, with capture listeners on the way down.

concepts.title: Event delegation
concepts.summary: One listener on a parent can handle events from many children, using event.target to find which one.

concepts.title: fetch promise
concepts.summary: fetch resolves with a Response for any HTTP status and rejects only when the request itself fails.

concepts.title: response.ok
concepts.summary: ok is true for status 200 to 299, and code must check it before trusting the body.

concepts.title: JSON
concepts.summary: JSON is text with double-quoted keys and strings, and stringify drops undefined, functions and symbols from objects.

concepts.title: Same-origin policy
concepts.summary: A page can read responses only from its own origin (scheme, host and port) unless the server opts in with CORS headers.

concepts.title: Web storage
concepts.summary: localStorage and sessionStorage keep string key-value pairs in the browser, the first until cleared and the second until the tab closes.

concepts.title: Cookies
concepts.summary: Cookies are sent to the server on matching requests, so they carry sessions, and flags such as HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite restrict how they travel.

concepts.title: Cross-site scripting
concepts.summary: If untrusted text is parsed as HTML, an attacker's script runs with the page's authority.

concepts.title: Safe sinks
concepts.summary: textContent inserts text as text, while innerHTML parses markup and so must never receive untrusted input.

concepts.title: Contrast ratio
concepts.summary: Contrast is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) from the lighter and darker relative luminances, from 1:1 to 21:1, and WCAG AA asks for 4.5:1 for normal text.

concepts.title: Keyboard access
concepts.summary: Everything operable by mouse must be reachable and usable by keyboard, in a logical focus order, with a visible focus indicator.

concepts.title: Core Web Vitals
concepts.summary: Largest Contentful Paint measures loading, Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness and Cumulative Layout Shift measures visual stability.

concepts.title: What slows a page
concepts.summary: Bytes, blocking scripts and styles, and late-discovered images delay first paint, and fixes include compression, defer and explicit image dimensions.

lessons.title: What the browser receives

lead.text: The **scheme**, `https`, names the protocol the browser will speak, and after the `://` comes the **host**, `shop.example.com`, the name of the machine to contact. The **port**, 8443, says which door on that machine to use; when the address leaves it out, the browser uses the scheme's usual one, 443 for https and 80 for http.

The **path**, `/items/42`, names a resource on the server, the **query** after the `?` is a list of `name=value` pairs joined by `&`, here `color=red` and `size=m`, and the **fragment** after the `#` names a place, here `reviews`.

reveal.text: The request on a later screen shows the answer in full: look for the part that has no place in it.
Each pair is a name and a value, and the server reads the pairs one by one to decide which items to return.

lead.text: Before anything can be asked, the browser needs a number to send it to. It asks a **DNS server** to turn the host name into an address, which is the first view of the figure, and then it connects to that address on the port. The message it sends is plain text, shown in the second view: the first line holds the **method**, here `GET`, which means fetch, then the path and query exactly as they appeared in the address. A **header** on the next line, `Host`, carries the host and the port, because a single machine can serve many sites and needs to be told which one is meant.

The reply is also text. It opens with a **status line** that holds a three-digit **status code**, then some headers, one of which, `Content-Type`, says what the body is, then a blank line and the **body** itself. When you request a page the body is the HTML.

diagram.alt: A sequence diagram with three views. First the browser asks a DNS server for the address of shop.example.com and gets back a number. Then it sends a request whose first line is GET /items/42?color=red&size=m and a Host header. Then the server replies with a status line, headers and the HTML text.
diagram.caption: The three messages before anything is drawn. Use the buttons to move through them.

steps.headline: Read the request for https://shop.example.com:8443/items/42?color=red&size=m#reviews, line by line.

workedSteps.text: The first word of the first line is the method, and GET asks the server to send back whatever lives at the path.
Next on the line comes the target, which is the path with its query attached, copied from the address.
The address ended with #reviews, and the target stops before it.
The server still needs to know which site on the machine is meant, so the host and port go in a header.
Together the message is a line and a header.

reveal.text: The next screen sorts status codes into families by their first digit, and 404 falls into one of them.

lead.text: Status codes are grouped by their first digit. A code that begins with 2 reports success, and 200 OK is the ordinary reply with the page in its body. A code that begins with 3 is a **redirection**: 301 Moved Permanently sends the browser to a new address, and 304 Not Modified says the copy it already holds is still good.

Codes that begin with 4 mean the *request* was at fault: 400 Bad Request means the server could not make sense of it, 401 Unauthorized that it needs a login, 403 Forbidden that the login does not allow it, and 404 Not Found that nothing exists at the path. Codes that begin with 5 mean the *server* failed: 500 Internal Server Error is the general one.

afterFigure.text: Every one of these is a response, which means a server was found, connected to and spoke, whereas a dead connection produces no status line at all.

diagram.alt: A table of status code families: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx a fault in the request, 5xx a fault in the server, each with example codes.
diagram.caption: Every row is an answer from a server that was reached.

reveal.text: Redirections are how an old address keeps working after a page moves.
The next screen explains the rules the parser follows, which are the same in every browser.

lead.text:
The body of the response is only text. The browser reads it from left to right with a **parser**, a program that follows a grammar to turn text into structure, and the structure it produces is the **DOM tree**: each element is a *node*, and an element written inside another becomes its child. The HTML standard says exactly what the parser does at every character, including when the text is wrong. The rule for `p` is that a new `p` tag closes any `p` still open, which is why `

One

Two` builds two sibling paragraphs and not one inside the other.

Other rules supply elements that the text never wrote. In the figure the file has table, tr and td, but a table's rows have to sit in a section, so the parser creates a tbody between the table and its row.

afterFigure.text:
The parser never refuses a page. Whatever the text contains, the standard defines a tree for it, and every browser builds the same one. The tree, not the file, is what appears on screen, so `

One

Two` and `

One

Two

` look different in an editor and build identical trees. When CSS picks an element or JavaScript changes one, it is working on the tree.

reveal.text: The table has a single child, the tbody that the parser added, and both rows sit inside it. CSS written for the table's first child will find a tbody and not a tr.
A missing end tag is repaired when the next element starts, and an end tag that is present closes only the element it names.

lessons.orientation: Follow a URL from the address bar to a request, a response and the tree the parser builds, and read the parts of a URL and a status code.
lessons.nextAction: Choose the HTML element that says what content is, and predict what a screen reader can navigate by.

blocks.text: Here is a web address: `https://shop.example.com:8443/items/42?color=red&size=m#reviews`. It is 63 characters long and looks like a single string, yet the browser reads it as six parts, each of which answers a different question about where to go and what to ask for when it gets there.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to split a URL into its parts, say what a status code's first digit tells you, and predict the tree the parser builds from a short piece of HTML.
intro.whyItMatters: The same chain of URL, request, response and tree sits under every page you will build or debug in the rest of the course.

recap.keyIdea: The browser turns a URL into a request, reads the server's status code as its answer, and builds a tree from the HTML in the body, repairing it by fixed rules.

blocks.text: A URL splits into scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment. The first four and the query shape the request, and the fragment stays in the browser, which is why changing it needs no request. The server's reply opens with a status code, and its first digit tells you whether the request succeeded, was redirected, or failed on the browser's side or the server's.

The body of that reply is parsed into a tree, and the parser repairs missing end tags and adds elements such as tbody by fixed rules. Because CSS and JavaScript both work on the tree and not on the text, the next lessons start from what the tree contains.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the elements in that tree and asks what each one says about the content inside it.

lessons.title: Structure and meaning

reveal.text: The next screen shows why: it lists what each kind of element gives a page for free.

lead.text: Here is a small news page built twice. In the first version every box is a `div`, an element that says only that something is a box, so a browser can draw the page but cannot tell the header from the story. In the second, the boxes are a **header**, a **nav** for the links, a **main** for the content, an **article** inside it and a **footer**. The text and the look can be identical, yet the second page says what each part is for, and that is what makes an element **semantic**.

A screen reader exposes the `header`, `nav`, `main` and `footer` as **landmarks**, and a person can jump from one to the next, which the third view of the figure lists. The `div` version offers nothing to jump to.

afterFigure.text: A button comes with keyboard focus, the role *button*, and activation by Enter and Space. A link comes with focus and the promise that activating it goes somewhere. A `div` has none of these until each is added by hand, so the choice of element is a choice about what the page can do for people who do not use a mouse.

diagram.alt: The same small page drawn two ways. In the first every box is a div, so nothing says what a box is. In the second the boxes are header, nav, main with an article, and footer. A third view lists the landmarks a screen reader offers: banner, navigation, main, contentinfo.
diagram.caption: One page, two markups, and the list a screen reader builds from the second. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: A heading element carries a level from 1 to 6, and the levels nest like the numbered parts of a report: an `h2` sits inside an `h1`, and an `h3` inside an `h2`. The level states a *position in the outline*.

Screen readers present the headings as a list that can be jumped through. The first view of the figure shows the list for a news page whose levels run 1, 3, 3, 2, 3. The first story is an h3 straight under the h1, so the outline has a gap where an h2 should be.

afterFigure.text: The rule is easy to state: a heading may be at most one level deeper than the heading before it, and it may return to any shallower level.

lead.text: Every control a person can use needs a name, because without one a screen reader can announce only its type: *edit text*, *button*. The **accessible name** is the text that software announces for a control. A button takes it from its content, so a button holding the text Save is named Save. An input has no content, so it takes its name from a **label**.

The tie is made by matching two attributes: the label's `for` must equal the input's `id`. In the figure the word Email beside the box is only nearby, which leaves the input unnamed, whereas `<label for="email">Email</label>` attached to `<input id="email">` makes the text part of the control's name.

afterFigure.text: The grey hint text inside an empty input is not a substitute. It disappears as soon as someone types, and it is not reliably announced as a name.

diagram.alt: An email input drawn twice. With only the word Email beside it, a screen reader announces edit text. With a label whose for matches the input's id, it announces Email, edit text, and clicking the word focuses the box.
diagram.caption: A label that is tied to its input becomes the input's name.

steps.headline: Work out the accessible name that each control below ends up with.

workedSteps.text: A button that contains the text Save takes its name from its content.
An input with the id email, and the word Email in plain text beside it, has no label tied to it, so it has no name.
A button holding only an image with an empty alt has no content to take a name from.
Now a label is added beside the input.

reveal.text: The next screen explains what each kind of alt text does for a reader who cannot see the image.

lead.text: The `alt` attribute on an `img` is the text that stands in for the picture when it cannot be seen: it is read by a screen reader, shown if the file fails to load, and used by search engines. It is not a caption, which sits beside the image for everyone, and it should say what the image *does* on the page.

A flourish between paragraphs gives a reader nothing, and the right `alt` for it is the empty string, `alt=""`, which tells software to skip the image. Leaving `alt` out is different from leaving it empty, since many screen readers then fall back to reading out the file name.

afterFigure.text: When an image sits inside a link that already contains the text Home, the link's name comes from the text, and an empty `alt` on the logo stops the page from announcing the same thing twice.

reveal.text: With alt text on the only image, the link is named by that text. Had the image carried an empty alt, as the logo beside the text Home did on the screen before, it would have added nothing to the name.
The same test sorts most controls: menus that navigate are links, and controls that change the page in place are buttons.

lessons.orientation: Choose the element that names what content is, and predict the landmarks, heading outline and names a screen reader will find.
lessons.nextAction: Work out the width and height of an element from its content, padding, border and margin, and predict how boxes flow and how vertical margins collapse.

blocks.text: Take the top of a news page, with a header, a menu of links and a story. Written with a div for each, the page has three boxes that the HTML does not tell apart, and written with a header, a nav and an article it has three parts that each say what they are. A browser draws the two identically from the same CSS, but a screen reader, a search engine and the browser's reader mode make sense of only the second, because none of them sees what a page looks like and each can use only what its elements say it contains.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose the element that says what a piece of content is, and predict what a screen reader can jump through or announce on a page.
intro.whyItMatters: Structure written into the HTML is what keyboards, screen readers and search engines can use, and CSS and JavaScript cannot add it back cheaply.

recap.keyIdea: An element should say what its content is, because assistive technology navigates and names a page by those roles and not by how it looks.

blocks.text: Elements such as header, nav, main and button name their content's role, so a screen reader can list landmarks and a keyboard can reach and operate controls without extra code. Heading levels form an outline whose levels should follow the real nesting, with size left to CSS.

Every control needs an accessible name, which a label tied by for and id supplies for an input, and an image needs alt text that stands in for it, empty when the image is decoration. In each case the question to ask is what the content does, and then to choose the element that says so.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to how the browser lays those elements out: the box each one occupies and the way boxes flow down a page.

lessons.title: The box and the flow

reveal.text: The next screen builds the box layer by layer, and you can check your number against it.

lead.text: Whatever an element contains, the browser lays it out as a rectangle, and the rectangle has four layers. At the centre is the **content**, the box that holds the text or the children. Around it is the **padding**, space inside the element that keeps the content from touching the edge and that shows the element's background. Around the padding is the **border**, a line of a chosen thickness, and around the border is the **margin**, empty space that keeps other elements away.

The lines beneath it add the layers up from the inside: each layer widens the box on *both* sides, so the padding adds 40 to the content's 200, the border adds 10 more, and the margin adds a final 30.

steps.headline: Find the border box and the margin box of an element with content 160px wide, padding 12px at each side, a 3px border and a 20px margin.

workedSteps.text: Start with the content, which is the declared width, since by default a width covers the content alone.
The padding adds 12 on the left and 12 on the right.
The border adds 3 on each side, which completes the border box.
The border box is now complete, and the margin lies outside it.

lead.text: The sums above rest on a default: when a width is declared, it describes the content box only. This is the value **content-box**, and it means that `width: 200px` with padding and a border produces an element wider than 200px, here 250px. The consequence is awkward for layout, because adding padding to an element makes it grow, and a column set to 50% wide stops fitting beside another once it has a border.

Setting **box-sizing: border-box** changes what the width means. The declared 200px then covers the content, the padding and the border together, so the element stays 200px wide and the *content* gives way, shrinking to 200 - 40 - 10 = 150px.

afterFigure.text: Neither value changes the margin, which is outside the border box under both. Many stylesheets set border-box on every element for this reason, since the width written in the rule is then the width the element takes.

diagram.alt: Two bars drawn to scale for a box declared width: 200px with padding 20 and border 5. Under content-box the content is 200 wide and the whole border box is 250. Under border-box the whole border box is 200 and the content shrinks to 150.
diagram.caption: The same declared width, two meanings. Use the buttons to switch box-sizing.

reveal.text: Had the element used content-box instead, the same declarations would have given a border box of 354px, wider than the 300px declared.

lead.text: Before any layout is chosen, the browser places boxes by one default scheme, called **normal flow**. A **block** box, such as a paragraph or a heading, starts on a new line and stretches to fill the width of its container, so successive blocks stack from top to bottom. An **inline** box, such as a `span`, a link or a word of text, sits within a line the way a word does, taking only the width of its content and wrapping to the next line when the line is full.
A block honours its width, height and vertical margins. An inline box ignores a width or height set on it, and its vertical margins do not push lines apart, because the line is what is being filled.

afterFigure.text: The display property switches a box from one kind to the other.

diagram.alt: Two views of normal flow. Block boxes are bars that each start on a new line and fill the width, stacked from top to bottom. Inline boxes sit in a line like words, with one highlighted span, and wrap to the next line when the line is full.
diagram.caption: How boxes flow when nothing else changes the layout. Use the buttons to compare block and inline.

cases.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 640 220"><defs><marker id="hf2" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="4" orient="auto"><path class="f-ink" d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z"/></marker></defs><text class="t" x="60" y="56" text-anchor="start">Inline boxes sit in a line, like the words of a sentence.</text><rect class="f-accent-soft s-accent w2" x="58" y="70" width="80" height="34" rx="6"/><text class="t" x="70" y="94" text-anchor="start">a span</text><text class="t" x="150" y="94" text-anchor="start">is one of them, and wraps with the text.</text><text class="t-small t-muted" x="320" y="190" text-anchor="middle">Inline boxes fill a line, then continue on the next.</text></svg>

reveal.text: An inline box gives up both: it shares a line with its neighbours and takes only the width of its content.
The next screen explains what the browser does when two vertical margins meet.

lead.text: Padding and borders always add, so it is natural to expect margins to add too, and it is the reverse for vertical margins in normal flow. When the bottom margin of one block meets the top margin of the next, the two share the same space and the gap is **the larger of the two**. This is called **margin collapse**. In the figure the 30px margin below paragraph A and the 20px margin above paragraph B overlap, and the ruler reads 30.

It affects only *vertical* margins, since left and right margins always add. It happens only between boxes in normal flow, which is why the children of a flex or grid container, met in the lesson on layout, do not collapse. Padding and borders never collapse, so a block with padding keeps its own space.

afterFigure.text: A page of paragraphs each given `margin: 1em` above and below would otherwise have double spacing between every pair and half spacing at the ends. Collapsing gives an even rhythm without anyone doing arithmetic.

diagram.alt: Two stacked paragraphs with their margins shaded and a ruler at the right showing the gap between them. With margins of 30 and 20 the gap is 30. With margins of 20 and 20 the gap is 20.
diagram.caption: The shaded margins overlap, and the ruler shows the gap that results.

reveal.text: The smaller margin is absorbed completely, so removing it changes nothing about the layout.
Each pair contributes one collapsed gap, and the margins at the very top and bottom of the stack lie outside the span you measured.

lessons.orientation: Compute the width an element occupies from its layers and its box-sizing, and predict the gap between stacked blocks.
lessons.nextAction: Rank competing CSS declarations by origin, importance, specificity and order, and say which values are inherited.

blocks.text: Open a browser's developer tools and select any element, and it is drawn as a set of nested rectangles: the content in the middle, then the padding, the border and the margin around it. A rule such as `width: 200px` gives the size of one of those rectangles, and which one it gives decides how much room the element takes, so that two elements with the same declared width can occupy quite different amounts of space.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to calculate the width an element occupies under content-box and border-box, and predict the gap between stacked blocks.
intro.whyItMatters: Most layout surprises in CSS come from a width that means something other than what it appears to, or a gap that is not the sum of two margins.

recap.keyIdea: An element is content, padding, border and margin, each outside the last, and box-sizing decides which of those layers a declared width covers.

blocks.text: An element is a rectangle of content, padding, border and margin, and each layer widens the box on both sides. Under content-box a declared width covers only the content, so 200px of content with 20px padding and a 5px border gives a border box of 250px, and under border-box the same 200px covers all three and leaves 150px of content.
In normal flow, block boxes stack and inline boxes fill lines, and vertical margins between block siblings collapse to the larger of the two, so 30px over 20px leaves a gap of 30px.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks which of several competing CSS rules decides an element's width, colour or margin when more than one applies.

lessons.title: Which rule wins

reveal.text: The next screen counts what each selector contains, and that count decides before the order of the rules does.

lead.text: Two rules often set the same property on the same element, and the browser has to pick one declaration. The first thing it compares is the **specificity** of each selector, a score of three counts. The first count is the number of ids, such as `#nav`. The second counts classes, attribute selectors such as `[href]` and pseudo-classes such as `:hover`. The third counts element names such as `a`, and pseudo-elements such as `::first-line`. The selector `#nav .item a:hover` therefore scores (1, 2, 1), as the first view of the figure shows.

To compare two scores, read them from the left. The first column that differs decides, and the columns after it are never looked at. In the second view `.btn.primary` scores (0, 2, 0) and `div .btn` scores (0, 1, 1): the ids tie, the classes differ, and the first selector wins, whatever the order in which the two rules were written.

afterFigure.text: The counts are compared, and never added into one number. One id, (1, 0, 0), therefore outranks any quantity of classes, which can seem wrong until you see that each column is its own place, like digits in a number where the left one is worth more. The universal selector `*` and the combinators such as `>` and a space add nothing.

diagram.alt: Two views of specificity. The first splits the selector #nav .item a:hover into an id, a class, an element and a pseudo-class, giving the counts 1, 2 and 1. The second compares .btn.primary scoring 0, 2, 0 with div .btn scoring 0, 1, 1: the classes column decides, so the first wins.
diagram.caption: A selector scores three counts, compared from left to right. Use the buttons for counting and comparing.

steps.headline: Score the selector .card:hover > p::first-line by counting each piece in its own column.

workedSteps.text: There is no #, so the ids column holds nothing.
.card is a class, and :hover is a pseudo-class, which sits in the same column.
The `p` is an element name, and `::first-line` is a pseudo-element, which sits in the elements column. The `>` only joins the parts and adds nothing.
That fills all three columns.

reveal.text: The same count tells you how hard this rule will be to override later.

lead.text: Specificity is only one rung of the cascade. The full decision runs down a ladder, shown in the figure, and the first rung that separates two declarations settles it. At the top a declaration marked **!important** beats an ordinary one whatever the selectors. Below that a **style attribute** written on the element itself beats any selector, since it is attached to that element directly. Then comes specificity, and only when two selectors score exactly the same does the **order of the rules** decide, with the later one winning. One rung is left off this ladder: a stylesheet that groups its rules into cascade layers with `@layer` has the layers compared before specificity, and this course does not use them.

Your rules also meet the browser's own default styles, which is why a link is blue and underlined before you write anything. Everything you write beats those defaults, regardless of specificity, because the browser's styles come from a different origin and rank lower.

afterFigure.text: Because !important and inline styles can be beaten only by more of the same, each use makes the next rule harder to write, and stylesheets that rely on them tend to escalate. Keeping selectors short and flat, and letting order break ties, leaves the cascade easy to predict.

diagram.alt: A ladder of four rungs that decides which declaration wins, strongest first: an important declaration, a style attribute on the element, selector specificity, and the rule written later. A note says the browser's default styles lose to every rule the author writes.
diagram.caption: Work down the ladder; the first rung that separates two declarations decides.

cases.label: The ladder

Browser default styles lose to every rule you write.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The id wins because its column is further left, and adding more classes only changes the column to its right.
The next screen explains which properties pass down to descendants and which do not.

lead.text: For some properties the children take the parent's value unless a rule of their own says otherwise, which is called **inheritance**. Setting `color` on `body` therefore colours the text of every paragraph, list item and heading beneath it without a rule for each, and `font-family` behaves in the same way.
The properties that inherit are mostly the ones about text. Those about an element's own box, such as border, margin, padding and background, do not.

afterFigure.text: The link is the exception that people notice. The browser's default stylesheet gives `a` a colour of its own, and a rule aimed at an element directly outranks any inherited value, so the link stays blue until you set its colour. An inherited value is the weakest kind there is.

diagram.alt: A small tree: body with children p and ul, p with child a, and ul with child li. In the first view body sets color: green, and p, ul and li inherit it while the link a keeps the browser's link colour. In the second view body sets a border and none of its descendants has one.
diagram.caption: Colour is passed down the tree and borders are not. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The p never sees the body's value, because the div's rule has already replaced it on the way down.

lead.text: A **custom property** is a name beginning with two hyphens, such as `--accent`, that holds any value, and `var(--accent)` reads it elsewhere. Custom properties are inherited like colour, so a value set on `:root` is available everywhere, and redefining it on one element changes it for everything inside that element.

The other tool is a pair of pseudo-classes that take a list of selectors. In **:is()** the specificity is that of the most specific selector in the list, so `:is(.a, #b) p` scores (1, 0, 1). In **:where()** it is always zero, so `:where(.a, #b) p` scores only the (0, 0, 1) of the `p`. A base style written with `:where()` is easy to override later, because anything written afterwards outranks it.

reveal.text: Redefining `--gap` on `.box` leaves every other part of the page on the `:root` value.
Writing `:where()` in its place would have given (0, 1, 0), the score of the `.title` class alone.

lessons.orientation: Score a selector, decide which of two rules wins, and say which properties are inherited.
lessons.nextAction: Predict item sizes in a flex row from basis, grow and shrink, and in a grid from fr units, gaps and fixed tracks.

blocks.text: An element can match many CSS rules at once, but a link has only one colour, so whenever two rules set it the browser has to choose. Suppose a link is matched both by `a { color: blue }` and by `.nav a { color: red }`: only one of the two declarations can apply, and the browser picks it by a fixed ranking called the **cascade**, which weighs how important each declaration is, how specific its selector is and where its rule sits in the stylesheet.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to score a selector, say which of two competing rules wins and why, and say which properties pass from parent to child.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every stubborn CSS bug is one rule losing to another, and the ranking is a procedure you can run by hand.

recap.keyIdea: The cascade ranks declarations by importance, then by the specificity of the selector, then by order, and some properties inherit from a parent.

blocks.text: The browser picks one declaration per property by working down a ladder: an important declaration first, then a style attribute, then selector specificity, and last the order of the rules. A selector scores three counts, ids then classes then elements, compared from the left and never added, so one id beats any number of classes.

Where no rule applies, text properties such as `color` and `font-family` are inherited from the nearest ancestor that sets them, and box properties such as `border` are not. Custom properties inherit too, and `:where()` and `:is()` change the score a selector contributes.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses the box model to lay out elements in a row and in a grid, with flexbox and grid.

lessons.title: Layout with flexbox and grid

reveal.text: The next screen shows that grow shares only the space that is left over.

lead.text: A **flex container**, set with `display: flex`, lays its children in a row along its **main axis**. Each item starts from its **flex-basis**, its ideal width before any adjusting, which is the item's width when none is given. If the basis widths add up to less than the container, the difference is the **free space**, and each item's **flex-grow** says how many shares of it the item takes.

In the figure the container is 600px wide and three items have a basis of 100px, so 300px is free. Grow factors of 1, 2 and 3 make six shares of 50px, and the items take one, two and three of them on top of their basis, ending 150, 200 and 250px wide, which add back to 600.

afterFigure.text: The factor does not set a width. A grow of 3 means three shares of what is left, so the same factor on the same item gives a different width in a wider container. Any gap between items comes off the free space before it is shared.

diagram.alt: A flex row drawn to scale in two views. First, a 600 wide container holds three items of basis 100 with 300 of free space left over. Second, with grow factors 1, 2 and 3 the items become 150, 200 and 250 wide.
diagram.caption: Basis first, then free space is shared by grow, or overflow is removed by shrink.

steps.headline: A 720px row holds three items with flex-basis 100px and flex-grow 1, 2 and 3. Find each width.

workedSteps.text: The bases add to 300px, so the free space is the rest of the container.
The grow factors add to six shares, so one share of the free space is the free space divided by six.
The first two items take one and two shares, added to their bases.
The third item takes three shares of the same size.

lead.text: Three items with a basis of 150px in a 300px row need 450px, so they overflow by 150px, and each item's **flex-shrink** says how much of that overflow it gives up. With the default factor of 1 and equal bases, each of the three loses a third of the overflow, 50px, and ends 100px wide, as the figure shows.

An item's share of the overflow is its shrink factor times its basis, divided by the sum of that quantity over all the items, which means a larger item loses more than a smaller one and the items keep their proportions. Because items cannot shrink below their content, a row of unbreakable text can still overflow.

diagram.alt: A 300 wide flex container holding three items of basis 150. They overflow by 150, and when shrunk each loses 50 and ends 100 wide.
diagram.caption: Overflow is shared out by shrink, and each of the three items gives up the same amount here.

reveal.text: The three items end up equal, since each started equal and each loses the same.

lead.text: Where flexbox works along one axis, a **grid container**, set with `display: grid`, defines both columns and rows, called **tracks**. The property `grid-template-columns` lists the columns, and each can be a fixed size such as 100px or a share of the free width written in **fr** units. The gap between tracks is set with `column-gap` or `gap`.

The browser takes the gaps and the fixed tracks out of the width first, and the fr units split what is left. With columns 1fr 2fr 100px and a 20px gap in an 800px grid, two gaps take 40px and the fixed column 100px, which leaves 660px for three parts: 220px for each fr, so the columns are 220, 440 and 100px.

afterFigure.text: That is why 1fr is not a share of the whole container. A grid whose fixed columns and gaps grow gives the fr tracks less to share, so the fr columns shrink to make room.

diagram.alt: A grid 800 wide with columns 1fr, 2fr and 100px and a gap of 20. The first view takes off the two gaps and the fixed track, leaving 660 to share. The second shows the columns 220, 440 and 100 with the gaps between them.
diagram.caption: The fixed track and the gaps come off first, and the fr units share the rest. Use the buttons to compare the steps.

steps.headline: A 900px grid has grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 140px and column-gap: 20px. Find the width of each column.

workedSteps.text: Three columns have two gaps between them.
The fixed column and the gaps come off the width first.
The fr tracks share the 720px as 1 + 2 = 3 parts.
The 1fr column is 240px, which is one part of the three.

reveal.text: The gaps are counted between tracks, so a grid with n columns has n - 1 of them.
The next screen compares the two modes by the number of dimensions they control.

lead.text: Flexbox asks how a single line of items should share its space, and the items decide a good deal of the result themselves through their basis. Wrapping onto another line is allowed, but each line is arranged on its own, so the items on a second line do not line up with those above.

Grid asks the opposite question. The columns and rows are planned first, and the items are put into the cells, so a column stays the same width on every row. This is what a page frame, a photo wall or a calendar needs, whereas a navigation bar, a row of buttons or a list of tags is a single line of content-sized items.

afterFigure.text: A useful test for any layout is to count how many dimensions have to line up.

diagram.alt: Two layouts of six items. As a flex row that wraps, tags keep their own widths and the two lines do not line up. As a grid, six equal cells sit in three columns and two rows that line up.
diagram.caption: Flex arranges one line at a time, and grid sets columns and rows for all of the items together.

The larger item gave up more, 40px against 20px, and in both cases the two losses add up to the 60px of overflow.

lessons.orientation: Work out flex item widths from basis, grow and shrink, and grid column widths from fr units and gaps, and choose between flex and grid.
lessons.nextAction: Convert rem, em, percent and viewport units to pixels, and decide which media query rules apply at a given viewport width.

blocks.text: Three boxes sit in a row inside a container 600px wide, each box is 100px wide, and the 300px that is left over has to go somewhere. Flexbox and grid are the two modern layout modes in CSS, and each answers that question with a rule that can be written as a short sum: flexbox shares the leftover space among the items according to numbers set on them, and grid divides a row's width among columns that are declared in advance.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out item widths in a flex row from basis, grow and shrink, work out column widths in a grid from fr units and gaps, and choose between the two.
intro.whyItMatters: Page layout is the part of CSS people most often fix by trial and error, and the sums replace the guessing.

recap.keyIdea: Flexbox shares leftover space or overflow along one axis from each item's basis, grid shares the width left after fixed tracks and gaps among fr tracks, and the choice depends on whether one dimension or two must line up.

blocks.text: In a flex row each item starts at its basis. Free space is shared in proportion to flex-grow, and overflow is removed in proportion to flex-shrink times basis, so 600px with three bases of 100px and grow factors 1, 2 and 3 gives widths of 150, 200 and 250px.

In a grid the gaps and fixed tracks come off the width and the fr tracks share the remainder, so 800px with columns 1fr 2fr 100px and a 20px gap gives 220, 440 and 100px. Flexbox suits a single line of content-sized items, and grid suits layouts whose rows and columns must line up.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how these layouts respond when the viewport changes size, using relative units and media queries.

lessons.title: Responsive design

reveal.text: The next screen shows what rem is measured from, and how it differs from em.

lead.text: A **rem** is the font size of the root element, which is 16px unless it is changed, so 1.25rem is 20px and 1.5rem is 24px wherever the element sits. An **em** is measured from the font size around it. On the `font-size` property that means the *parent's* size, so a parent of 20px with a child of 1.5em gives 30px, and a grandchild of 1.5em inside that gives 45px, because each level multiplies the one above, as in the figure.
A **percentage** width is a share of the containing block's width, so 60% of a 350px container is 210px. A **vw** is one hundredth of the viewport's width, so 5vw is 60px on a viewport 1200px wide.

afterFigure.text: Because rem looks only at the root, changing one value there rescales the whole page, whereas em suits lengths that should follow the element's own text, such as the padding on a button. On properties other than font-size, em is measured from the element's own font size.

diagram.alt: Two sets of nested boxes. With rem, a parent of 1.25rem is 20px on a 16px root and a child of 1.5rem is 24px, both measured from the root. With em, a parent of 20px, a child of 1.5em and a grandchild of 1.5em give 20, 30 and 45px, each measured from the one above.
diagram.caption: rem is always measured from the root, and em compounds down the nesting. Use the buttons to compare.

steps.headline: Convert these lengths to pixels on a viewport 1200px wide, with a 16px root and a container 480px wide.

workedSteps.text: A rem is the root font size, so 1.25rem is 1.25 times 16.
A vw is one hundredth of the viewport, which is 12px here, so 5vw is five of them.
A width of 50% is half the container.
Now a box is given a width of 75% in that same container.

reveal.text: Each condition is tested separately, and more than one can be true at once.

lead.text: A **media query** wraps some rules in a condition, such as `@media (min-width: 600px)`, and the browser applies them only while the condition holds. The condition is about the **viewport**, the visible area of the page, and not about the device: it is tested at the moment the page is shown and again whenever the window is resized. A `min-width` of 600px is true for any viewport at least 600px wide, and a `max-width` of 600px is true for any viewport at most that wide, with the limits included.

The usual way to write a responsive page is **mobile first**. The base rules describe the narrowest layout, here a single column, and `min-width` queries add to them as room appears. In the figure the base rules give one column at 320px, the 600px block makes two at 700px, and the 900px block makes three at 1000px, with no JavaScript involved.

diagram.alt: A viewport ruler from 300 to 1200 pixels with breakpoints marked at 600 and 900, and a page thumbnail below it. At 320 the page is one column and only the base rules apply. At 700 it is two columns because min-width 600 applies. At 1000 it is three columns because both min-width queries apply.

reveal.text: The list shows that conditions are independent: any number of them, from none to all, can be true at one width.

lead.text: A rule inside a media query has the same specificity as the same rule outside it, so when several blocks apply at once the ladder from the lesson on the cascade falls through to the **order of the rules**. With `min-width` queries written smallest first, each larger breakpoint is written after the smaller ones and overrides them as the viewport grows, which is what makes the layered result predictable. At 1200px in a stylesheet with `.card` at 100%, then 60% from 500px, then 25% from 800px, all three rules apply and the last of them, 25%, wins.

A 500px block placed after the 800px block still applies on a wide viewport, and since it comes later it overrides the larger breakpoint, so the wide layout never appears. One more line is needed on a phone: the viewport meta tag, with `width=device-width`. Without it a mobile browser lays the page out at a wide virtual width and shrinks the result, and the media queries would be tested against that wide width.

reveal.text: Every rule written here matches the 1000px viewport, so only the order separates them.
The 900px rule is still correct for wide viewports, and it is hidden because a rule for a narrower breakpoint comes after it.

lessons.orientation: Convert relative units to pixels, and decide which media query rules apply at a given viewport width.
lessons.nextAction: Predict the result of an expression that mixes strings, numbers, booleans, null, undefined and arrays, using the language's conversion rules.

blocks.text: A phone 360px wide and a laptop 1280px wide can be sent the same HTML and the same stylesheet and still show one column and three. The stylesheet makes the difference itself, in two ways: some of its lengths are measured from something that varies, such as a percentage of the container or a hundredth of the viewport, and some of its rules sit inside a condition, such as `@media (min-width: 600px)`, that holds only while the viewport is at least 600px wide.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert rem, em, percent and vw lengths to pixels, and say which media query rules apply at a given viewport width.
intro.whyItMatters: One stylesheet that behaves correctly from a phone to a wide monitor depends on these conversions and on the order of the breakpoints.

recap.keyIdea: Relative units are measured from a reference, and media queries test the viewport, so a stylesheet can be read at any width by working out the units and the conditions.

blocks.text: A rem is measured from the root font size and an em from the font size around it, so em values compound down the nesting, while a percentage follows the container and a vw follows the viewport. With a 16px root, 1.25rem is 20px, and 1.5em inside 1.5em inside 20px is 45px.

A media query applies its rules while its condition on the viewport is true, with min-width and max-width limits included. Mobile-first stylesheets write the base for the narrowest screen and add min-width blocks in increasing order, because blocks of equal specificity are settled by order.

recap.nextHook: With the document and its styling covered, the next lesson starts on JavaScript and the rules by which it converts values from one type to another.

lessons.title: Values, types and coercion

reveal.text: The next screen follows each expression one step at a time.

lead.text: Type `'5' + 3` into a browser console and it prints 53, and type `'5' - 3` and it prints 2. JavaScript converts a value to another type when an operator needs one, and this is called **coercion**. The rule for `+` is that if either operand is a string, the other is converted to a string as well and the two are joined, so the 3 becomes `'3'` and the result is the string `'53'`.

The other arithmetic operators have no meaning for text. `-` and `*` and `/` convert *both* operands to numbers, so `'5' - 3` becomes `5 - 3` and gives 2, and `'3' * '4'` gives 12. The conversions follow fixed rules: `true` becomes 1, `false` becomes 0, and `null` becomes 0, while `undefined` becomes `NaN`, a value that means not a number.

afterFigure.text: The practical hazard is that a value read from a page, such as the text typed into an input, is always a string, so adding it to a number joins instead of adding unless it is converted first.

diagram.alt: Two expressions evaluated in steps. For '5' + 3, one operand is a string, so the number 3 becomes the string '3' and the two are joined, giving the string '53'. For '5' - 3, subtraction turns both sides into numbers and gives the number 2.

steps.headline: Work out what console.log('4' + 2 * 3) prints, one operation at a time.

workedSteps.text: Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so it runs first and both of its operands are numbers.
The + now has the string '4' on its left and the number 6 on its right.
One operand is a string, so the 6 becomes '6' and the two are joined.
The expression has been reduced to a single join.

reveal.text: The same conversion explains why a count of true values can be found by adding them.
The next screen lists every primitive type with what typeof gives for it.

lead.text: A value is one of seven **primitive types**: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null` and `symbol`. Everything else, including arrays and functions, is an object. The `typeof` operator reports the type as a string, and the figure lists what it gives for each. Its answer for `null` is `'object'`, an error in the first version of the language that was never corrected because pages depended on it, so `null` has to be tested with `=== null`.

Explicit conversion avoids the surprises of coercion. `Number('')` is 0, but `Number('12px')` is `NaN`, because `Number` rejects any string that is not entirely a number. `parseInt('12px')` is 12, since `parseInt` reads as many digits as it can and stops at the first character that does not fit. Where a boolean is needed, as in an `if`, a value is read as **truthy** or **falsy**, and only eight values are falsy: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, the empty string, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. The string `'0'` and an empty array are truthy.

reveal.text: Only the values on the list are falsy. Here `undefined` and `0n` are on it, and `-1`, 'false', `{}` and a space are not, so those four are truthy.
The next screen sets `==` beside `===` and follows one of these conversions step by step.

lead.text: The strict operator `===` answers a simple question: are the two values of the same type and the same value? There is no conversion, so `1 === '1'` is `false`. The loose operator `==` converts first, following rules that are easiest to read as a series of steps. In the second view of the figure `[] == false` becomes `'' == 0` and then `0 == 0`, which is `true`, although an empty array and the boolean `false` have little in common.

Two further rules are worth knowing. `null` and `undefined` are loosely equal to each other and to nothing else, so `null == undefined` is `true` while `null == 0` is `false`. `NaN` is not equal to anything, itself included, so `NaN === NaN` is `false`, and the reliable test is `Number.isNaN(x)`.

afterFigure.text: Use `===` and `!==` by default, convert explicitly where you need a conversion, and use `== null` in the one place where you want to catch both `null` and `undefined`.

reveal.text: Writing `x == null` in a condition is the one use of `==` that many style guides allow, since it catches both null and undefined and nothing else, false included.

lead.text: Every number in JavaScript is a 64-bit floating-point value, which stores a number as a binary fraction. A fraction such as one half, a quarter or three quarters is a sum of powers of two, so it is stored exactly. A tenth is not, in the same way that one third has no finishing decimal: 0.1 is stored as a slightly larger number, about 0.1000000000000000055, and 0.2 as a slightly larger one still.

The sum of those two, 0.1 + 0.2, is stored as 0.30000000000000004, and the literal 0.3 is stored as a slightly smaller number, so `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false`. The limit applies to whole numbers too, since integers are exact only up to 2^53 - 1, which is 9007199254740991.

afterFigure.text: The remedies are to compare with a tolerance, to count in whole units such as pence instead of pounds, and to format with `toFixed` when displaying: `(0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2)` is `'0.30'`.

diagram.alt: Two tables of stored numbers. The first shows that 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are stored with small errors, so 0.1 + 0.2 is stored as 0.3000000000000000444 while 0.3 is stored as 0.2999999999999999889. The second shows that 0.5, 0.25 and 0.75 are stored exactly, so 0.5 + 0.25 equals 0.75.
diagram.caption: Decimal fractions such as 0.1 have no exact form in binary, and fractions built from halves do. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: The difference is 0.19999999999999998, a hair below 0.2, which is too small to see when printed with toFixed(2) and large enough for === to fail.

lead.text: The default sort converts the values it compares to strings.

reveal.text: The same array sorted with `(a, b) => a - b` gives `[ 1, 9, 10 ]`, because a comparison function sorts by number.

lessons.orientation: Predict what expressions mixing strings, numbers, booleans, null and arrays evaluate to, choose between == and ===, and explain float results.
lessons.nextAction: Trace which variable a name refers to across function, block and closure scopes, including hoisting and the var-in-loop trap.

blocks.text: The `7` in an expression and the `'7'` in quotes look alike on screen, but the first is a number and the second a string, and JavaScript treats them as different values: `7 === '7'` is `false`, and a form field that contains the text 7 hands your code the string. When types do not suit an operator, JavaScript converts one or both values to a type that does and carries on, a step called **coercion**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict what an expression mixing strings, numbers, booleans, null and arrays evaluates to, choose between == and ===, and explain why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3.
intro.whyItMatters: Many bugs in real pages come from a value that was a string when the code assumed a number, and the rules say exactly where that happens.

recap.keyIdea: JavaScript converts operands by fixed rules: `+` joins if either side is a string, the other arithmetic operators produce numbers, `===` compares without converting, and numbers are binary floating point.

blocks.text: The `+` operator joins when either operand is a string, and `-` `*` and `/` convert both operands to numbers, so `'5' + 3` is `'53'` and `'5' - 3` is 2. Seven primitive types exist, `typeof null` is `'object'` for historical reasons, and only eight values are falsy.

The strict operator `===` compares type and value without converting, whereas `==` converts first and gives results such as `[] == false` being `true`. Numbers are 64-bit binary floating point, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 and why integers are exact only up to 9007199254740991.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to functions, and to which variable a name refers to inside them.

lessons.title: Functions, scope and closures

reveal.text: The next screens explain where the variable lives and why it survives.

lead.text: Every function, and every block in braces, creates a **scope**, a region in which the names declared inside it are available. When a line uses a name, the engine looks in the scope that contains the line, then in the one around that, and so on out to the global scope, and it uses the first declaration it finds. This is called **lexical scope**, because the lookup follows where the code is *written* and not where it is called from.

If a function declares its own `x`, then inside that function `x` means the function's variable, and the outer `x` with the same name is hidden from it. The second view of the figure shows this, which is called **shadowing**, and the outer variable is not changed in any way.

afterFigure.text: The declarations let and const belong to the nearest block, and var belongs to the nearest function.

diagram.alt: Three nested rings: global scope, function scope and block scope. In the first view code in the block looks up step in its own ring, total one ring out in the function, and rate two rings out in the global scope. In the second view an x in the function hides the global x, so code in the block finds the function's x.
diagram.caption: Lookup moves outward from where the code was written. Use the buttons to compare finding a name and hiding one.

The lookup stops at the nearest.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The function's own x and the outer x are two variables that happen to share a name.

lead.text: A function is not only code but code together with the scope in which it was created. When `makeAdder(3)` returns an inner function, `makeAdder` itself has finished, yet the inner function can still read and change the variable `total` that `makeAdder` declared, and the variable stays alive for as long as that function does. This combination is called a **closure**.

Each call of `makeAdder` creates a new `total`. In the figure `u = makeAdder(3)` and `v = makeAdder(10)` share the same code but hold separate variables, so calling `u` twice and `v` once leaves the totals at 6 and 10. The closure holds the *variable itself*, not a copy of its value at the time the function was made, so a later change is seen the next time the function runs.

afterFigure.text: Closures are the usual way in JavaScript to keep private state, such as a counter, between calls without any global variable.

diagram.alt: Two adders made by calling makeAdder with the steps 3 and 10. Each is a function that keeps its own private total. Initially both totals are 0. After u twice and v once they are 6 and 10. After one more u they are 9 and 10.

steps.headline: Trace p = makeAdder(5) and q = makeAdder(2) through p(); p(); q(); and then console.log(p(), q()).

workedSteps.text: Each `makeAdder` call creates its own `total`, which starts at 0 and goes up by the call's step each time it is called.
The first two calls of p add 5 each.
The call `q()` adds 2 to the `total` of `q` alone.
`console.log` then calls `p()` again, which makes 15, and calls `q()` again.

reveal.text: Neither counter ever sees the other, since each `makeCounter` call made its own `n`.
The next screen sets the three kinds of declaration side by side.

lead.text: Before it runs a scope, the engine reads its declarations, so names exist earlier than their lines do, a behaviour called **hoisting**. A function declaration is hoisted with its whole body, so `f` can be called above the line that declares it. A `var` is hoisted without its value, so it holds `undefined` until its assignment runs, and `typeof g` is `'undefined'` in the example.

A `let` or `const` is different again. It belongs to its block from the start, yet any use before its line throws a `ReferenceError`, and the stretch between the start of the block and that line is called the **temporal dead zone**. The error is deliberate: reading a variable before it has a value is almost always a mistake, and an error shows it at once, whereas `undefined` would let it pass.

afterFigure.text: In practice you rarely need to rely on hoisting: declare a name before you use it, and prefer let and const to var.

diagram.alt: Three rows describing what happens when a name is used before its declaration line has run. A function declaration is usable and typeof f is function. A var holding a function expression exists with the value undefined. A let or const throws a ReferenceError.
diagram.caption: The three kinds of declaration behave differently before their line runs.

reveal.text: The other three print a value, which is why bugs with var can go unnoticed.
The next screen shows how many variables are in play.

lead.text: The scheduled callbacks are closures, and each one keeps the variable i. With var the variable belongs to the surrounding function, so the loop has exactly one i, and it counts up to 3 before any callback runs. All three callbacks read that one variable and print 3.

A let in the head of a for loop is created fresh for each iteration, with the value carried over from the last one, so there are three separate variables holding 0, 1 and 2, and each callback closes over its own. That is the second view of the figure, and it prints 0 1 2.

afterFigure.text: This is the main reason to prefer let.

diagram.alt: Three callbacks created in a loop of three iterations. With var, all three point at one shared variable i whose value is 3 after the loop. With let, each callback points at its own i, holding 0, 1 and 2.
diagram.caption: var gives the loop one variable, and let gives each iteration its own. Use the buttons to compare.

The answer would be the same if the change came from inside another function, since both refer to one variable.

lessons.orientation: Trace which variable a name refers to across function, block and closure scopes, including hoisting and the var-in-loop trap.
lessons.nextAction: Predict when two names share one object, what a spread copy does and does not copy, and what array methods return or mutate.

blocks.text: A function can use a name that it never declares itself. In `let rate = 0.2; function tax(price) { return price * rate; }`, the name `rate` is not declared inside `tax`, so JavaScript looks for it in the code around the function and finds the variable on the first line. The search always runs outward from where the code is written, whether the function is called there or from somewhere else entirely, and this one rule, called **lexical scope**, decides what every name in a program refers to.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to trace which variable a name refers to across nested scopes and closures, and predict the output of hoisting and loop-callback examples.
intro.whyItMatters: Closures and scope sit behind event handlers, timers and most JavaScript libraries, and they cause a well-known family of loop bugs.

recap.keyIdea: A name is resolved outward from where the code was written, and a function keeps the variables of the scope it was created in, so closures keep the variable and not a copy.

blocks.text: A name is resolved by looking outward from where the code is written, and an inner declaration hides an outer one of the same name. A function keeps the variables of the scope that created it, even after that scope has returned, and each call that creates the scope makes a fresh set, so two counters have independent state.

Declarations are hoisted: a function declaration works before its line, a var holds undefined, and a let or const throws until its line has run. A var in a loop gives every callback the same variable, which is why a loop of three timers prints 3 3 3, whereas let gives each iteration its own and prints 0 1 2.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at objects and arrays, and at when two names refer to the same object.

lessons.title: Objects, arrays and references

reveal.text: The next screen shows what each name holds.

lead.text: A number or a string is copied when it is assigned, but an array or an object is not. A variable that holds one actually holds a **reference** to it, and an assignment such as `t = s` copies the reference. The result is two names for one array, drawn in the first view of the figure, so a `push` made through `t` is seen through `s`, and `s.length` becomes 3. The same happens when an array or object is passed to a function, since the parameter is another name for it.

To get a second array, one has to be made, as `[...s]` does in the second view. A `const` fixes the *binding*, meaning the name cannot be made to refer to something else, but it does not freeze what the name refers to, so a `const` array can still be pushed to.

diagram.alt: Two views of names and arrays. In the first, the names s and t both point at one array holding x, y and z, because assigning t = s copies the reference. In the second, t = [...s] creates a second array, so s still holds x and y while t holds x, y and z.
diagram.caption: A name holds a reference to the array, and an assignment copies the reference. Use the buttons to compare an alias with a copy.

reveal.text: The other three lines change the array and leave the binding alone, which is why they are allowed.

steps.headline: Trace p = { n: 1 }, then q = p, then q.n = 5, then r = { ...p }, then r.n = 9.

workedSteps.text: p names an object holding n: 1.
`q = p` copies the reference, so `q` names the same object, and `q.n = 5` changes that one object.
The spread builds a new object with a copy of each top-level value, so r holds n: 5 and is separate.
`r.n = 9` changes only `r`.

reveal.text: The next screen shows what a spread copy duplicates.

lead.text: The spread syntax `{...o}`, and its relative `Object.assign`, makes a new outer object and copies each of its properties into it. If a property holds a number or a string, the copy gets its own value. If it holds an object, what is copied is the *reference*, so the copy and the original both point at one inner object. In the first view of the figure, `c.x.y = 2` reaches through the shared `x` and changes the object that `o` also uses, so `o.x.y` reads 2. This is called a **shallow copy**.

When the inner objects must be independent too, a **deep copy** is needed. The built-in function `structuredClone(o)` copies the whole structure, including nested objects and arrays, so the second view shows the original left alone. The cost is that `structuredClone` cannot copy everything: it rejects functions, for instance.

afterFigure.text: A practical rule: spread is enough for a flat object, and anything with objects nested inside needs either a deep copy or a copy at each level that you change.

diagram.alt: Two views of copying the object o = { x: { y: 1 } }. With a spread copy c, the outer objects differ but both x properties point at one shared inner object, so c.x.y = 2 changes it for o as well. With structuredClone the inner object is copied too, so o keeps y of 1.
diagram.caption: Spread copies the top level only. Use the buttons to compare it with a deep copy.

reveal.text: The next screen sorts the methods into the two groups.

lead.text: The array methods fall into two groups. `push`, `pop`, `splice`, `sort` and `reverse` **mutate** the array they are called on, which changes every name that refers to it. `slice`, `map`, `filter`, `concat` and `toSorted` return a *new* array and leave the original as it was, as the figure shows.

The method that most often catches people is `sort`. It reorders the array in place and also returns that same array, so `const sorted = n.sort()` leaves two names for one reordered array, and the original order is gone. Sorting a copy keeps the original, with `[...n].sort()` or with `toSorted()`, which returns a new sorted array.

diagram.alt: Two columns of array methods. Those that change the array in place are push, pop, splice, sort and reverse. Those that return a new array and leave the original alone are slice, map, filter, concat and toSorted.
diagram.caption: Check which column a method is in before relying on the original array.

reveal.text: Had the copy been made with `b = a` instead, both names would have shown the sorted order.

lead.text: Three methods cover most work on arrays, and each returns a new value without changing the array. `map(f)` calls `f` on every item and returns an array of the results, with the same length. `filter(f)` calls `f` on every item and keeps those for which it returns a truthy value. `reduce(f, start)` carries a running value through the array: `f` receives the running value and the next item and returns the new running value, which ends as the result.

The figure works on `[5, 6, 7]`: `map(n => n * 2)` gives `[10, 12, 14]`, `filter(n => n > 10)` keeps `[12, 14]`, and `reduce` with a sum starting at 0 gives 26. One detail matters for callbacks: `map` passes each function three arguments, the item, its index and the array, so a function that accepts extra arguments will receive them.

diagram.alt: A pipeline on the array [5, 6, 7]. map(n => n * 2) gives [10, 12, 14]. filter(n => n > 10) keeps [12, 14]. reduce with a sum starting at 0 gives the single number 26.
diagram.caption: Each stage takes the array from the one before. Use the buttons to follow the stages.

lessons.orientation: Say when two names share one object, what a spread copy copies, and which array methods mutate.
lessons.nextAction: Predict the order in which synchronous code, promise callbacks, await continuations and timers run.

blocks.text: In JavaScript `[1, 2] === [1, 2]` is `false`, although both sides hold the same two numbers. The variable that names an array holds a **reference** to it, a record of where the array is, and `===` asks whether two references lead to the same array. Each pair of brackets above builds a new array, so the two sides lead to different ones, whereas numbers and strings are compared by their values, which is why `1 === 1` is `true`.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say when two names share one object, what a spread copy does and does not copy, and which array methods mutate and which return a new array.
intro.whyItMatters: Shared references are behind some of the most confusing bugs in JavaScript, because a change in one place shows up in another.

recap.keyIdea: Names hold references to objects and arrays, so assignment shares them, a spread copy is shallow, and array methods either mutate in place or return something new.

blocks.text: Assigning an array or object copies a reference, so two names can point at one thing and a change through either is seen through both. `const` fixes the name and leaves the object changeable. A spread or `Object.assign` copy duplicates only the top level, so nested objects stay shared, and `structuredClone` copies the whole structure.

`push`, `pop`, `splice`, `sort` and `reverse` change the array in place, while `slice`, `map`, `filter`, `concat` and `toSorted` return a new one. `map`, `filter` and `reduce` chain, so `[1, 2, 3, 4]` doubled, filtered above 4 and summed gives 14.
