lessons.title: The event loop and promises

reveal.text: The next screen shows what the program is doing while the timer waits.

steps.headline: The stack and the task queue

lead.text: JavaScript runs on a single thread, so only one piece of code runs at a time, and it runs to the end before anything else starts. The place where running functions are tracked is the **call stack**. A function call goes onto the stack, anything it calls goes above it, and each comes off as it returns. While the stack holds something, nothing else can run, and that includes callbacks that other code has asked for.

Those callbacks wait in a **task queue**. `setTimeout` asks the browser to put a callback in the queue after a delay, so with a delay of 0 the callback is still only *queued*. The **event loop** is the rule that connects the two: when the stack is empty, take the next task from the queue and run it. In the figure the script prints `x` and `z` first, and only after it has finished does the loop take the timer's callback, which prints `y`.

afterFigure.text: A zero delay therefore means as soon as possible after the current code, and never in the middle of it. Timers also wait for their delay in order of due time, so a timer set for 0 comes before one set for 100 even if it was written second.

diagram.alt: The call stack and the task queue for a program that logs x, sets a zero-delay timer that logs y, and logs z. First the script runs and prints x and z while the timer callback waits in the task queue. When the stack is empty the timer callback runs and prints y.
diagram.caption: A zero-delay timer queues a task. It does not run until the script has finished. Use the buttons to compare the two moments.

reveal.text: No timer runs before the script has finished, whatever its delay, and after that the shortest delay runs first.
The next screen introduces a second queue, which decides the answer.

lead.text: A **promise** stands for a value that is not ready yet. It starts *pending* and is settled exactly once, as *fulfilled* with a value or *rejected* with an error, and then the callbacks given to `then` and `catch` are run. They are not run at that moment: they go into a second queue, the **microtask queue**, which the event loop empties completely whenever the stack becomes empty, before it takes the next task from the task queue.

The figure shows a program that prints A, sets a timer that prints T, queues a callback P1 that queues a second callback P2, and prints B. The script prints A and B. The microtasks then run, P1 and then P2, which was added while the queue was draining and runs before the loop moves on. The timer's task runs last, so the output is A B P1 P2 T.

afterFigure.text: The rule is the same for every program: the script, then all the microtasks, then one task, then all the microtasks again, and so on. It explains why a promise callback queued *after* a timer still runs before it.

diagram.alt: The event loop in three moments for a program that logs A, sets a zero-delay timer that logs T, queues a promise callback P1 that queues P2, and logs B. First the script runs and prints A and B while P1 and the timer wait. Then the microtasks run, printing P1 and P2. Last the timer task runs and prints T.
diagram.caption: Order of output: A B P1 P2 T. Use the buttons to step through the three moments.

reveal.text: `queueMicrotask` adds directly to the microtask queue, where a promise callback would go.

steps.headline: Trace the order of output when a microtask queues another microtask while a timer is waiting.

workedSteps.text: The script queues a zero-delay timer that will print t1, queues a promise callback that will print m1, and prints s. At the end of the script the stack empties.
The first microtask runs and prints m1, and while it runs it queues a second microtask that will print m2.
The first microtask has finished, and the timer's task is still waiting.
When both queues are empty, the output is complete.

lead.text: An **async function** returns a promise, and inside it the keyword **await** waits for another promise. A call to the function runs like any other, step by step, until it reaches its first `await`. At that point the function is *suspended*: its place is kept, the call returns to its caller, and the rest of the function is queued as a microtask to resume when the awaited promise settles. With `await null` the promise is already settled, so the function resumes as soon as the stack is empty.
In the figure g prints g1 and reaches the await. The script carries on and prints h2, and only then does g resume and print g2, so the output is h1 g1 h2 g2.

afterFigure.text: Code that comes before the first await in an async function runs synchronously, which surprises people who expect the whole function to be delayed.

diagram.alt: An async function g that logs g1, awaits null and logs g2, called between two logs h1 and h2. Output is h1, g1, h2, g2. The call to g runs up to its await and prints g1. The script carries on and prints h2. Then g resumes from the microtask queue and prints g2.
diagram.caption: await pauses only the async function, and the rest of the program runs on. Use the buttons to follow the three moments.

lessons.orientation: Predict the output order of programs that mix synchronous code, timers, promise callbacks and await.
lessons.nextAction: Select and change nodes, and predict the order and target of events as they capture down and bubble up through nested elements.

blocks.text: If a script keeps the browser busy for two seconds, a button clicked during that time does nothing until the script is done, and then its handler runs. JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time, to the end, and anything that happens in the meantime, such as a click, a timer running out or a reply arriving from a server, leaves a callback waiting for its turn.
Which waiting callback runs next is decided by a fixed rule, called the **event loop**, which keeps more than one queue and takes from them in a set order.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict the order of output of a program that mixes synchronous code, timers, promise callbacks and await.
intro.whyItMatters: Every web page waits for something, a click, a timer or a server, and the order in which those callbacks run explains many bugs.

recap.keyIdea: JavaScript runs the script to completion, then all queued microtasks, then one task from the task queue, then the microtasks again, and await resumes the function as a microtask.

blocks.text: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time to completion, tracked on the call stack, and callbacks wait in queues. A timer's callback is a task, so even a delay of 0 runs only after the current script. Promise callbacks are microtasks, and the whole microtask queue, including anything queued while it runs, is emptied before the next task.

await suspends only the async function that contains it and resumes it as a microtask, so the rest of the program carries on in between. Applying the order script, microtasks, one task, microtasks gives 1 4 3 2 for the program that logs 1, sets a zero-delay timer, queues a promise callback and logs 4.

lessons.title: The DOM and events

lead.text: The tree from the first lesson is available to JavaScript as the **DOM**, with the page as the object `document`. To find an element, `document.querySelector('ul')` takes any CSS selector and returns the first match, and `querySelectorAll` returns all of them. To change one, `textContent` sets its text, `setAttribute` sets an attribute, and `classList.add` or `classList.remove` change its classes. To add and remove elements, `document.createElement` makes a new one, which is not in the page until `append` or insert puts it in the tree, and `remove` takes one out.

Every piece of the tree is a **node**, and the whitespace between tags is a node as well, a text node. The property `childNodes` lists *every* child node, whitespace included, whereas `children` lists only the *elements*. An `ol` with three `li` elements, written on separate lines with indentation, has 3 `children` and 7 `childNodes`, because four text nodes sit before, between and after the items, as the first view of the figure shows.

afterFigure.text: Use `children` when you want the elements, and `childNodes` only when text and comments matter.

lead.text: A click is not delivered only to the element that was clicked. The event first travels *down* from the root to the target, which is the **capture phase**, then it is delivered at the target, and then it travels back *up* through each ancestor, which is the **bubble phase**. Listeners added in the usual way, with `addEventListener('click', f)`, run in the bubble phase, so a click on a button in `div#inner` in `div#outer` fires the button's listener, then inner's, then outer's, as the first view of the figure shows.

A listener added with a third argument of `true`, `addEventListener('click', f, true)`, runs in the capture phase instead. A capture listener on outer therefore fires *first*, before anything at the target, as in the second view. Inside a listener, the method **stopPropagation()** ends the journey, so no later element hears the event, as in the third view.

afterFigure.text: `stopPropagation` and `preventDefault` do different jobs. `stopPropagation` stops the event travelling to other elements, whereas `preventDefault` cancels what the browser would do itself, such as following a link or submitting a form, and a listener may need one, both or neither.

diagram.alt: A button inside div#inner inside div#outer, with the order in which click listeners fire. Bubbling only: button, inner, outer. With a capture listener on outer: outer capture first, then button, inner, outer. With stopPropagation called in inner: button, then inner, and outer does not fire.
diagram.caption: An event goes down to its target and then back up. Use the buttons to compare three setups.

reveal.text: The capture listener on inner comes first because the event reaches inner on the way down, before it reaches the button.
The button's listener logs button and then ends the journey, so inner and outer never hear the click.

lead.text: Because events bubble, a listener does not have to be on the element that was clicked. A single listener on a `ul` hears the clicks from all its `li` elements, so a list of fifty items needs one listener rather than fifty, and items added later are covered as well. This is called **event delegation**.

Inside the listener, two properties tell the parts of the event apart. **event.target** is the element where the event began, such as the `li` that was clicked, and **event.currentTarget** is the element the listener is attached to, here the `ul`. If the click lands on something inside the `li`, such as a `span`, the target is that `span`, and code that wants the item uses `event.target.closest('li')` to climb to it.

afterFigure.text: Delegation depends on the event bubbling, which is why an event that stops propagation early can silently disable a delegated listener above it.

lessons.orientation: Count nodes, order nested event listeners, and tell event.target from event.currentTarget.
lessons.nextAction: Read fetch code and predict what happens on a 404, a network failure and a repeated body read, and write and read JSON correctly.

blocks.text:
The browser builds a tree from the markup `

Hello world

` in which the paragraph has two children, the text Hello with its trailing space and the element `b`, and the `b` has one child of its own, the text world. JavaScript reaches that tree through the **DOM**, and every item in it, text as well as elements, is a node, so a script that searches a page, reads it, changes it or counts its parts is working on nodes.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the nodes under an element, predict the order in which nested click listeners fire, and say what event.target and event.currentTarget refer to.
intro.whyItMatters: Every interactive page is built on finding elements and handling events, and ordering mistakes there cause bugs that are hard to see.

recap.keyIdea: The DOM is a tree of nodes that includes whitespace text, and an event travels down to its target and back up, which lets one listener on a parent serve all its children.

blocks.text: The DOM is a tree of nodes with methods to find, change, add and remove them. `childNodes` counts every child node, whitespace text included, and `children` counts only the elements, so a list of two items written over four lines has 5 `childNodes` and 2 `children`.

An event captures down the tree to its target and then bubbles back up, so listeners on ancestors fire too, in the order outer capture, target, then each ancestor outward. `stopPropagation` ends that travel, and a delegated listener on a parent reads `event.target` for the source and `event.currentTarget` for the element the listener is on.

lessons.title: Talking to servers

reveal.text: The next screen follows three outcomes of a fetch call, and 404 is one of them.

lead.text: The `fetch` function asks for a resource and returns a promise of a **Response**. The promise settles when the reply's headers arrive, and what counts as success may surprise you: it resolves for *every* status code, a 404 and a 500 included, because in each case a server did reply. It rejects only when the request itself fails, as when the host cannot be reached or the connection drops.

A `Response` has a status, the number from the status line, and **ok**, which is `true` for statuses 200 to 299 and `false` otherwise. Code that goes straight to the body without checking `ok` will try to read an error page as though it were what it asked for. The reliable pattern is to await the fetch, check `ok`, and only then read the body.

afterFigure.text: Network failures, by contrast, throw, so a try and catch around the await handles them.

diagram.alt: Three paths through a fetch call. If the server replies with status 200 the promise resolves, ok is true and json gives the data. If it replies with 404 the promise still resolves but ok is false, so the code must check. If no response arrives the promise rejects and the catch block runs.
diagram.caption: fetch rejects only when no response arrives. Use the buttons to follow three outcomes.

steps.headline: Write a fetch call that reads JSON safely, one step at a time.

workedSteps.text: Start the request and wait for the response. The promise resolves for any status.
A 404 or 500 has resolved here too, so the status has to be checked before the body is read.
The check is a single line that throws for any other status, so the code after it can trust the response.
Only now is the body read and parsed as JSON. This is also a promise.
A network failure would already have thrown at the first line, so a try and catch around all three covers both faults.

lead.text: A response body is a stream, and a stream is consumed as it is read.

reveal.text: Cloning the response before reading gives two bodies, each of which can be read once.
The next screen lists the values that JSON cannot express and what stringify does with each.

lead.text: Servers and pages exchange data as text, and the usual format is **JSON**. It looks like a JavaScript object, with some strict rules: keys and strings use *double* quotes only, there are no trailing commas, and the only values are objects, arrays, strings, numbers, `true`, `false` and `null`. `JSON.stringify` turns a value into that text, and `JSON.parse` turns the text back into a value, throwing a `SyntaxError` for text that breaks the rules, such as single-quoted strings.

An object property holding undefined, a function or a symbol is left out. In an array the same values become null, since the array must keep its length. NaN and Infinity become null, and a Date becomes an ISO text string, so JSON.parse gives back a string, not a Date.

diagram.alt: A table of what JSON.stringify does with values it cannot represent. undefined, functions and symbols are left out of objects and become null in arrays. NaN becomes null in both. A Date becomes an ISO text string in both.
diagram.caption: Several values do not survive stringify. The text is only what JSON can express.

The next screen defines an origin and shows pairs that match and pairs that do not.

lead.text: An **origin** is the combination of scheme, host and port. `https://a.com` and `https://a.com:443` are the same origin, because 443 is the default port for https, while `http://a.com` differs in the scheme, `https://b.a.com` in the host and `https://a.com:8443` in the port. The path and the query never matter.

Browsers apply the **same-origin policy**: code on a page can read responses only from its own origin. A request to another origin may still be *sent*, but the script cannot read the reply unless the other server opts in, which it does by sending CORS headers such as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.

afterFigure.text: The practical consequence is that a CORS error appears in the browser console while the same request works in a command-line tool, since a tool has no such policy.

diagram.alt: A table of four pairs of URLs. https://a.com and https://a.com:443 share an origin because 443 is the default for https. http://a.com differs from https://a.com by scheme, https://b.a.com differs from https://a.com by host, and https://a.com:8443 differs from https://a.com by port.
diagram.caption: An origin is the scheme, the host and the port taken together.

blocks.text: A page that wants data asks for it with a call such as `fetch('/items/42')`, gets back a response that carries a status code, some headers and a body, and reads the body as JSON, a text format that looks like a JavaScript object but follows stricter rules. Each of those steps has details that are easy to read wrongly: what counts as success for a request, what survives the trip into text and back, and which replies the browser allows the page's script to read at all.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to read fetch code and say what happens on a 404, a network failure and a repeated body read, predict what JSON.stringify writes, and decide whether two URLs share an origin.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every page that loads data uses fetch and JSON, and the mistakes in this lesson are the ones that appear in real code.

recap.keyIdea: `fetch` rejects only when no response arrives, so code must check `response.ok`, and JSON and the same-origin policy each have fixed rules about what is kept and what may be read.

blocks.text: `fetch` resolves with a `Response` for any status, so a 404 or 500 is an ordinary resolved promise with `ok` `false`, and the promise rejects only when no response arrives. A response body can be read once, which is why `json()` a second time throws and why `clone()` exists.

JSON.stringify leaves out undefined, functions and symbols in objects, writes them as null in arrays, turns NaN into null and a Date into text, and JSON.parse throws on text that breaks the format. An origin is the scheme, host and port together, and a page can read a response only from its own origin unless the server opts in through CORS.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson covers where a page can keep data between visits, and why putting user text into the page needs care.

lessons.title: Storing state and trusting input

reveal.text: The next screen shows what storage returns for several kinds of value.

lead.text: The browser can keep small amounts of data for a page in **web storage**. `localStorage` keeps it until it is cleared, even after the browser is closed, and `sessionStorage` keeps it until the tab is closed. Both work with `setItem(key, value)`, `getItem(key)` and `removeItem(key)`, and both are tied to an origin so another site cannot read them.

The values are *always strings*. `setItem('n', 5)` stores the text `'5'`, so `getItem('n')` returns `'5'` and adding 1 to it gives `'51'`, as the first row of the figure shows. A boolean becomes the text `'true'` or `'false'`, and an object becomes `'[object Object]'`, which loses its contents. The way round it is the pair from the last lesson: `JSON.stringify` on the way in and `JSON.parse` on the way out. A key that was never stored returns `null`.

afterFigure.text: The text 'false' is a non-empty string and therefore truthy, so a stored flag has to be compared with the string and not tested directly.

diagram.alt: Four rows showing what storage returns. Storing the number 5 gives back the string '5'. Storing true gives back 'true'. Storing an object gives back '[object Object]', which loses the contents. Storing JSON.stringify of the object gives back JSON text that JSON.parse can restore.
diagram.caption: Web storage keeps strings only. The last row shows the way round it.

steps.headline: Store the object { a: 1 } so that it can be read back with its structure intact.

workedSteps.text: Passing the object straight to `setItem` converts it to text first, and the text for any plain object is the same.
Convert the object to JSON text yourself, so that the structure is written down.
On reading, `getItem` returns the text, which `JSON.parse` turns back into an object.
After the parse, the restored object is a real object again, and its `a` is not text.

reveal.text: The next screen compares `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and cookies.

lead.text: A **cookie** is a small piece of data that the server asks the browser to keep, with a `Set-Cookie` header, and the browser then sends back in a `Cookie` header on every matching request. That is the difference that matters: web storage stays in the browser, whereas a cookie travels to the server, which is why cookies carry login sessions.

Three flags restrict a cookie. **HttpOnly** hides it from page scripts, so `document.cookie` cannot read it. **Secure** sends it only over HTTPS. **SameSite** limits whether it is sent on requests that begin on another site.

afterFigure.text: The consequence for a session token is that it belongs in an HttpOnly cookie. A token in `localStorage` can be read by *any* script on the page, so if an attacker ever gets code running there, the token goes with it.

diagram.alt: A comparison of localStorage, sessionStorage and a cookie. localStorage lasts until cleared, sessionStorage until the tab closes, and a cookie for the time its Max-Age sets. Script can read all three, except that an HttpOnly cookie is hidden from it. Only cookies are sent to the server with each request. Typical uses are preferences, per-tab state and a session id.
diagram.caption: Where the data lives and who can see it decide which to use.

reveal.text: The other two flags control how the cookie is sent, and neither stops a script from reading it.
The next screen explains what happens when text from a user reaches the page.

lead.text: Text that comes from outside the page, such as a comment, a name or a search term, cannot be trusted to be harmless. If the page puts it in with **innerHTML**, the browser *parses* it as markup, and a stranger who can write markup can write an `img` tag whose `onerror` attribute holds code. That code runs as part of the page, with the page's permissions: it can read what the page can read, send requests from the user's session and change what the user sees. This attack is called **cross-site scripting**, or XSS.

The remedy is to avoid the parser. Setting **textContent** inserts the characters as text, so `hi` appears as typed and the element gains no children, as in the figure. Trying to filter the markup by hand, by removing the word `script` or by escaping some characters, is fragile, since each trick you miss still works. Frameworks escape by default for the same reason, and a `Content-Security-Policy` header is a second line of defence, telling the browser which scripts it may run even if markup does slip through.

afterFigure.text: The rule is short: use `textContent` for text, and reach for `innerHTML` only with markup that you wrote yourself.

diagram.alt: Text from a user, hi, inserted two ways. With textContent it is shown as typed and the element has no child elements, so it is safe. With innerHTML it is parsed as HTML and becomes a real b element, which is unsafe if the text came from a stranger.
diagram.caption: textContent inserts text, and innerHTML parses it as markup. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Filtering and escaping by hand leave the parser in place, and so leave other ways in. Inserting the name as text means it is never read as markup.
The text node and the `b` element are the two children, which is the difference between `childNodes` and `children` from the DOM lesson.
Converting with Number first, as in `Number(sessionStorage.getItem('count')) === 0`, tests the number that was meant.

blocks.text: A call such as `localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark')` keeps a value in the browser, and the page finds it again after a reload and after the browser has been closed. Cookies keep data in the browser as well, and the places differ in how long the data lasts, whether it is sent to the server and which code can read it.
A comment typed by a stranger or a name taken from a link arrives from outside the page, and how it is put into the page decides whether it is shown as text or runs as code.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage for a job, predict what storage returns, and explain why textContent is safe where innerHTML is not.
intro.whyItMatters: Where a token is kept and how user text is inserted are the two decisions that most often turn a small page bug into a security hole.

recap.keyIdea: Web storage holds strings and any script can read it, session tokens belong in HttpOnly cookies, and untrusted text must go in as text with `textContent` and not through the HTML parser.

blocks.text: `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` keep strings only, `localStorage` until cleared and `sessionStorage` until the tab closes, so a stored 5 returns `'5'` and a missing key returns `null`. Cookies are sent to the server with matching requests, and an HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by script, which makes it the place for a session token.

`innerHTML` parses its input as markup, so putting untrusted text through it lets an attacker's markup run with the page's authority, which is cross-site scripting. `textContent` inserts text without parsing it, and that is the safe default for anything that came from outside.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson covers making a page usable by everyone and quick to load, with contrast ratios and the Core Web Vitals.

lessons.title: Accessible and fast

reveal.text: The next screen gives both and shows how the ratio is computed.

lead.text: You cannot judge contrast by eye, because a grey that looks clear on one bright monitor may be hard to read on another. The **contrast ratio** puts a number on it. Each colour has a **relative luminance** L from 0 for black to 1 for white, which weights the red, green and blue channels by how bright the eye finds each, and the ratio is (L of the lighter colour + 0.05) divided by (L of the darker + 0.05).

Level **AA** asks for 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text, which means 18 point or larger, or 14 point if bold. The figure draws six colours on white against the 4.5 line. `#767676` gives 4.54 and passes, the slightly lighter `#777777` gives 4.48 and fails, and `#888888`, which looks only a little lighter again, falls to 3.54.

afterFigure.text: Measure with a contrast checker, and do it for every text and background pair, including text on images and on buttons.

steps.headline: Compute the contrast ratio of the grey #595959 on white.

workedSteps.text: Both colours are greys, so their three channels are equal, and the relative luminance of white is 1.
The grey's channel 0x59 is 89 out of 255, which is 0.349, and the standard converts that to a linear value.
The lighter colour is white. Add 0.05 to each luminance.
The two terms of the ratio are now written out.

reveal.text: The result is only just above the line, which is why this grey is a useful one to remember.

lead.text: The Tab key moves **focus** from one control to the next in the order the elements appear in the document, and Enter or Space activates the one that has it. Only elements that are meant to be interactive take focus: links, buttons, form controls. A `div` with a click handler takes none, which is why the choice of element in the lesson on structure matters again here.

The order should match the reading order, so the layout should follow the document and not be rearranged with CSS in a way that sends focus jumping across the page. And focus must be *visible*. Browsers draw a ring around the focused element, and a stylesheet that removes it with `outline: none` and puts nothing in its place leaves a keyboard user unable to see where they are.

reveal.text: The div is the kind of control that works for a mouse user and is invisible to a keyboard user.
The next screen sets out the three Core Web Vitals.

lead.text: The **Core Web Vitals** measure what a user sees and feels. **Largest Contentful Paint**, LCP, is the time at which the largest image or block of text appears, a measure of loading, and it is good at 2.5 seconds or less. **Interaction to Next Paint**, INP, is how long the page takes to show a result after a click, tap or key press, a measure of responsiveness, and it is good at 200 milliseconds or less. **Cumulative Layout Shift**, CLS, adds up how much visible content moves unexpectedly, a measure of visual stability, and it is good at a score of 0.1 or less.

Each is judged at the *75th percentile* of real page loads, so a page is good only if three quarters of its visits reach the threshold. The figure draws the three scales, with a band for good, a band for needing work and a band for poor, the poor limits being 4 seconds, 500 milliseconds and 0.25.

afterFigure.text: A slow server or a huge image raises LCP, long scripts that block the page raise INP, and images that arrive late and push text down raise CLS.

diagram.alt: Three scales for the Core Web Vitals. Largest Contentful Paint measures loading and is good at 2.5 seconds or less, poor above 4. Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness and is good at 200 milliseconds or less, poor above 500. Cumulative Layout Shift measures stability and is good at 0.1 or less, poor above 0.25.
diagram.caption: Each vital has a good threshold, measured at the 75th percentile. Use the buttons to compare the three.

lead.text: Three kinds of cost delay what a user sees. *Bytes* come first: a larger file takes longer to arrive, which compression and smaller images reduce. *Blocking* is the second: a script or stylesheet that the parser must finish before it can go on holds back first paint, and the `defer` attribute on a script lets the page continue while it downloads. The third is *discovery*: an image that is only found late, perhaps after a script has run, arrives late, and the largest element is often an image.

An image with no size arrives and pushes the text below it down the page, as in the figure. The **layout shift score** is the *impact fraction*, the share of the viewport that the moved content covers before and after, multiplied by the *distance fraction*, how far it moved as a share of the viewport. The fix is to reserve space: with `width` and `height` attributes the browser works out the image's shape before the file arrives, and holds that room, scaling the reserved height to whatever width the image is shown at.

afterFigure.text: The same applies to adverts and banners that load late: give them a box of a fixed size, so that nothing below them has to move.

diagram.alt: A page before and after an image loads. With no space reserved, the text sits close under the heading and then is pushed down when the image arrives, which is a layout shift. With the image's size reserved by width and height, a dashed empty space is held and the image fills it, so the text never moves.
diagram.caption: A late image pushes content only if no space was kept for it. Use the buttons to compare.

blocks.text: Pure red, #ff0000, looks strong on a white page, yet its contrast ratio against white is 4.0 to 1, which is below the 4.5 to 1 that the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines ask for in normal-size text. The ratio comes from a formula applied to the two colours, so whether a pair passes is settled by calculation, however the page looks on one screen.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute whether a colour pair meets the contrast minimum, and name what each Core Web Vital measures and its good threshold.
intro.whyItMatters: Contrast and the vitals are the measurable parts of a good page, and both can be checked while you build it.

recap.keyIdea: Accessibility and speed have measurable thresholds: 4.5 to 1 contrast for normal text, and LCP of 2.5 s, INP of 200 ms and CLS of 0.1 for loading, responsiveness and stability.

blocks.text: The contrast ratio is (L of the lighter + 0.05) divided by (L of the darker + 0.05), and WCAG AA asks for 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text, so #767676 on white passes at 4.54 and #777777 fails at 4.48. Keyboard users need real controls, a sensible focus order and a visible focus ring.

The Core Web Vitals are Largest Contentful Paint for loading, good at 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint for responsiveness, good at 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift for stability, good at 0.1, each at the 75th percentile. Reserving space for images with width and height, deferring scripts and keeping files small address the causes.

questions.prompt: Which part of `https://shop.example.com:8443/items/42?color=red&size=m#reviews` is never sent to the server?
hints: Look at the request line in a request: which of the six parts could be missing from it?
The part marked by the # character.
questions.onCorrect: The fragment is read by the browser alone, which is how a link to #reviews can scroll a page without asking the server for anything.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The part after the # is the fragment, and the browser keeps it.

questions.prompt: How many name and value pairs does the query of `https://shop.example.com/search?q=lamp&colour=red&page=2` contain?
hints: Find the ? and read what follows it.
Pairs are separated by the `&` character.
Count the `=` signs, one for each pair.
questions.onCorrect: A query is a list of `name=value` pairs joined by `&`, and the server reads them to decide what to return.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the `&` characters. There is one more pair than there are separators.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The query is `q=lamp&colour=red&page=2`. The `&` characters separate three pairs: `q=lamp`, `colour=red` and `page=2`.

questions.prompt: Why is #reviews missing from the request line?
hints: Think about where a fragment is used: it names a place inside a page that has already arrived.
questions.onCorrect: The fragment names a place inside the finished page, so only the browser needs it.

misconceptions.feedback: The server never sees the fragment, so it has nothing to remove. The browser leaves it out of the message.
The Host header carries only the host and the port. The fragment is not sent in any header.

acceptedIdeas: The browser keeps the fragment for itself and uses it after the page arrives.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The browser keeps the fragment for itself and uses it after the page arrives.

choices.label: The server removes the fragment as soon as the request arrives.
The fragment travels in the Host header instead.
The browser keeps the fragment for itself and uses it after the page arrives.

questions.prompt: A request for a page returns the status 404. What does that tell you?
hints: A status code is part of a response. Where does a response come from?
The first digit sorts the code into a family.
questions.onCorrect: A 404 is a complete, working reply: the server was found and answered that the path leads nowhere.

misconceptions.feedback: A failed connection produces no response at all, so there is no status code to read. A 404 is a response.
A crash is a 5xx fault in the server. The 4 in 404 puts the fault in the request.
A blocked request never reaches the server, so no status line comes back.

acceptedIdeas: The server was reached and says it has nothing at that path.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The server was reached and says it has nothing at that path.

choices.label: The network connection failed before reaching the server.
The server crashed while handling the request.
The server was reached and says it has nothing at that path.
The browser blocked the request.

questions.prompt: A server replies 301 Moved Permanently and a Location header. In one word, what kind of status is this?
hints: Look at the first digit of 301.
The 3xx family has a name that describes what the browser does next.
questions.onCorrect: The browser follows a redirection by making a new request to the address in the Location header.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A 301 starts with 3, the family of redirections.

questions.prompt:
The parser reads `

One

Two` with no closing tags. What tree does it build?
hints: A p element cannot contain another p element.
What happens to an open p when a new p starts?
questions.onCorrect: A new p start tag closes any p still open, so the missing end tags change nothing about the tree.

misconceptions.feedback: A p element cannot contain another p. A new p start tag closes any p that is still open, so the second one is not nested.
The parser never refuses a page. The standard defines a tree for any text, including text with end tags missing.
Each p start tag begins its own element, so a second tag means a second p element and not more text in the first.

acceptedIdeas: Two p elements side by side, one holding One and one holding Two.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two p elements side by side, one holding One and one holding Two.

choices.label: A single p element holding the text One and Two.
Two p elements side by side, one holding One and one holding Two.
One p element holding One, with a second p nested inside it that holds Two.
No p elements, because the markup is invalid.

questions.prompt:
In the tree built from `
x
`, what is the tag name of the table's first child?
hints: The text has no element between table and tr, but the tree may.
Table rows live in a section element.
questions.onCorrect: The tree contains elements that the file never wrote, because the parsing rules supply them.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The parser inserts a tbody between table and tr, so the first child is TBODY.

questions.prompt:
The parser reads `

One

Two

Three

`. How many `p` elements are in the tree?
hints: Count the opening p tags.
A closing tag ends an element; it does not add one.
Each opening tag starts a new p, and a new p closes any p still open.
questions.onCorrect: One closing tag in the text does not change the count. Each opening p tag still starts its own element.

misconceptions.feedback: A closing tag does not merge the paragraphs. Each opening tag begins its own element.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each opening p tag starts a new element, and the final closing tag only ends the third one, so the tree has three.

questions.prompt: In `https://docs.example.org:3000/guide/intro?lang=fr#setup`, what is the path?
hints: The path comes after the port and before the ?.
Do not include the query or the fragment.
questions.onCorrect: The host and port say who to contact; the path and query say what to ask that server for.

misconceptions.feedback: The part from the ? onward is the query, which is a separate part of the address, and the path stops before it.
The host and the port come before the path and are parts of their own.
The query and the fragment are separate parts that follow the path. Neither belongs to it.

acceptedIdeas: /guide/intro, because the path stops where the ? begins
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: /guide/intro, because the path stops where the ? begins

choices.label: /guide/intro?lang=fr, because the path runs up to the #
/guide/intro, because the path stops where the ? begins
docs.example.org:3000/guide/intro, because the path starts at the host
/guide/intro?lang=fr#setup, because the path is everything after the port

questions.prompt: A response arrives with the status 503. What does it tell you?
hints: Look at the first digit.
4 is a fault in the request and 5 is a fault in the other family.
questions.onCorrect: A 5xx status means the server understood the request and failed to carry it out.

misconceptions.feedback: A failed connection produces no response at all, so there is no status code to read. A 503 is a reply.
A fault in the request is reported by a status that begins with 4. This one begins with 5.

acceptedIdeas: The server was at fault, so it could not carry out the request
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The server was at fault, so it could not carry out the request

choices.label: The connection failed, so no server was reached
The request was at fault, so the browser sent something the server could not use
The server was at fault, so it could not carry out the request

questions.prompt:
The parser reads `
  • A
  • B
  • C
`. How many `li` elements are in the tree?
hints: Every li start tag begins a new item.
An open li is closed when the next li starts.
Count the li start tags: A, B and C.
questions.onCorrect: The parser closes each li when the next one starts, so the tree holds three siblings.

misconceptions.feedback: The later li tags do not nest inside the first. Each one closes the one before it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each li start tag closes the previous li, so the list holds three li elements.

questions.prompt: A table has a delete control on each row. Which element should that control be, so that a keyboard user and a screen reader can both use it without extra work?
hints: Ask whether the control goes somewhere or does something.
One of these gives keyboard focus and Enter and Space activation for free.
questions.onCorrect: A button comes with focus, a role and activation by Enter and Space, none of which a div supplies.

misconceptions.feedback: A link goes somewhere. Deleting a row does something, and a link would announce itself as navigation.
A div has no keyboard focus and no role, so Enter and Space do nothing unless every part is added by hand.
The role says link, which promises navigation, and the span still has no keyboard focus.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: <button>

choices.label: `<div onclick>`
`<span role='link'>`
`<button>`

questions.prompt: Which element marks the one block that holds the main content of a page?
hints: Its name is the answer to the question.
questions.onCorrect: A screen reader lists main as a landmark, so a user can jump straight past the header and navigation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The main element holds the page's primary content, and a page should have just one.

questions.prompt: A page's headings, in order, are h1, h2, h4, h2, h3, h3, h5. Which of them skip a level compared with the heading before?
hints: Compare each heading with the one just before it, not with the first heading.
A heading may go at most one level deeper than the heading before it, and may return to any shallower level.
questions.onCorrect: The h4 follows an h2 and the h5 follows an h3, so each is two levels deeper than the heading before it. Every other heading stays level, goes one deeper or returns to a shallower level.

misconceptions.feedback: The h5 also skips a level. It follows an h3, and a heading may go at most one level deeper than the one before it.
Going back from the h4 to an h2 is allowed, because a heading may return to any shallower level. The rule limits only how far a heading may go deeper.
The first h3 comes straight after an h2, which is one level deeper and allowed. The h4 that follows the first h2 is the other heading that skips.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The h4 and the h5

choices.label: The h4, the second h2 and the h5
The first h3 and the h5
The h4 only
The h4 and the h5

questions.prompt: The input has the id email, and the page now adds a label element whose for is email and whose text is Email. What name does a screen reader announce for the input?
hints: The text of the matching label is used for the name.
questions.onCorrect: Labels also make the text clickable: clicking Email puts the cursor in the input.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The label's text becomes the input's accessible name, so the input is announced as Email.

questions.prompt: An img is a flourish drawn between paragraphs and carries no information. Which alt is correct?
hints: Decide what a reader who cannot see the image loses if it is skipped.
Ask which option lets software skip the image without announcing anything.
questions.onCorrect: An empty alt marks the image as decoration, so assistive technology skips it.

misconceptions.feedback: A screen reader would read that text aloud, interrupting the reader for something with no content.
With no alt at all, many screen readers read out the file name instead.
Announcing that an image is there adds noise and says nothing about what the image shows.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: alt="" (empty)

choices.label: `alt="image"`
`alt=""` (empty)
`alt="decorative flourish"`
no alt attribute

questions.prompt: A link contains an `img` with `alt=""` and the text Home. What accessible name does a screen reader announce for the link?
hints: The empty alt contributes no text.
questions.onCorrect: The link's name comes from its content, and the empty alt keeps the logo from being announced twice.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The empty alt contributes nothing, so the link's name comes from its text: Home.

questions.prompt: A control reveals a hidden panel on the same page and goes nowhere. Which element should it be?
hints: Ask whether the control goes somewhere or does something on the current page.
A link goes somewhere. Which element is for doing something?
questions.onCorrect: A control that does something on the current page is a button, and it comes with keyboard focus and activation by Enter and Space.

misconceptions.feedback: An a element promises that activating it goes somewhere. This control goes nowhere and instead does something on the page, which is the job of a button.
A div has no keyboard focus, no role and no activation by Enter or Space until each is added by hand, while a button comes with all three.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A button element

choices.label: An a element, since it is clicked like a link
A button element
A div with a click handler

questions.prompt: Which HTML element marks the block of links that lead to a site's other pages, such as Home, Products and Contact?
hints: It is the landmark that groups a page's menu of links.
questions.onCorrect: A page can have several nav elements, and each one appears in the landmark list.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The nav element marks navigation links, and a screen reader lists it as a navigation landmark.

questions.prompt: A page has three controls: ``, ``, and an `` with no label and no hint text. Which of them have no accessible name?
hints: A button takes its name from its content. What does each button contain?
An input has no content, so its name has to come from a label.
questions.onCorrect: Only the first button has text to take a name from. The empty alt gives the second button nothing, and the input has no label.

misconceptions.feedback: The button that holds only an image with an empty alt has no name either, because its content supplies no text for one.
A button takes its name from its content, and an image with an empty alt adds none, while an input with no label and no hint text has nothing to take a name from.
The button holding the text Add takes its name from that text, so it is named Add.

acceptedIdeas: The image button and the input
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The image button and the input

choices.label: All three
Only the input
The image button and the input
None of them

questions.prompt: A section under an h2 contains a subsection. Which heading element should the subsection's title use?
hints: Levels go down by one at a time.
questions.onCorrect: Choosing a level by the outline, and leaving size to CSS, keeps the heading list truthful.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A subsection sits one level below its parent, so under an h2 it uses h3.

questions.prompt: An element has `width: 300px`, `padding: 15px` on every side, `border: 3px solid` and `box-sizing: content-box`. How wide is its border box?
hints: Under content-box, which part of the box does width describe?
Does the padding sit inside the declared width or outside it?
questions.onCorrect: The declared width covers only the content, and the padding and border are added on both sides of it, so the border box is 300 + 2 x 15 + 2 x 3 = 336px.

misconceptions.feedback: Under content-box the declared width describes the content alone, and the padding and the border are added outside it, so the border box is wider than 300px.
That is what `box-sizing: border-box` does. Under content-box the 300px covers only the content, and the layers around it make the border box wider.

acceptedIdeas: More than 300px, because the padding and the border are added to the width
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More than 300px, because the padding and the border are added to the width

choices.label: Exactly 300px, the declared width
Less than 300px, because the padding and the border use up part of the width
More than 300px, because the padding and the border are added to the width

questions.prompt: Continue the worked example: with the 20px margin on each side, what is the width in px of the margin box?
hints: Start from the border box width, 190.
The margin goes outside the border, on both the left and the right.
Add 20 twice.
questions.onCorrect: The margin box is the outermost layer, and it reserves space around the element without being part of it.

misconceptions.feedback: The margin is added to both sides, so it contributes 20 + 20 = 40, not 20.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The border box is 190px and the margin adds 20px on each side, so 190 + 20 + 20 = 230px.

questions.prompt: An element has `box-sizing: border-box`, `width: 300px`, `padding: 0 25px` and `border: 2px solid`. What is its content width in px?
hints: Under border-box, width covers content, padding and border together.
Subtract the horizontal padding on both sides, then the border on both sides.
questions.onCorrect: Under border-box the declared width stays fixed, and the content gives way as padding and border grow.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole border box. The content is what remains after padding and border come out.
Under border-box, padding and border come out of the width and are not added to it.
The padding of 25 on each side also comes out of the 300.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Under `border-box` the 300px includes padding and border, so the content is 300 - 25 - 25 - 2 - 2 = 246px.

questions.prompt: Which display value makes a box start on a new line and stretch to fill the width available?
hints: Boxes of this kind stack from top to bottom.
questions.onCorrect: An inline box instead sits within a line, and its width and height are ignored.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A block box starts on a new line and fills the width of its container.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A has margin-bottom: 30px and the paragraph below it, B, has margin-top: 20px. Both are normal block siblings. What is the gap between them?
hints: Think about whether two margins that meet add or overlap.
When margins overlap, the space is shared between them.
questions.onCorrect: The two margins share the same space, so the larger one sets the gap.

misconceptions.feedback: The upper margin is the larger of the two. Where two vertical margins meet they share the space, and the larger one sets the gap.
Adjoining vertical margins in normal flow overlap and do not add, so the gap is set by the larger one.

acceptedIdeas: 30px, the same as the larger margin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 30px, the same as the larger margin

choices.label: 50px, the two margins added together
30px, the same as the larger margin
20px, the same as the smaller margin

questions.prompt: Paragraph A has margin-bottom: 24px and block sibling B has margin-top: 16px. What is the gap in px?
hints: Do the margins add or overlap?
Compare the two margins.
The larger one sets the gap.
questions.onCorrect: Whichever of the two is larger sets the gap, and the smaller one has no effect.

misconceptions.feedback: Sibling margins overlap and do not add. The larger one sets the gap.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The margins collapse to the larger, 24px.

questions.prompt: Three block paragraphs are stacked, each 30px tall with no padding or border and `margin: 20px 0`. How many px is it from the top edge of the first paragraph to the bottom edge of the third?
hints: Count the paragraph heights, then the gaps between them.
Each gap is where a bottom margin meets a top margin.
questions.onCorrect: Collapsing applies to every pair of adjoining siblings, so a stack of n blocks has n - 1 gaps of the single margin.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds both margins in each gap, 20 + 20, but adjoining margins collapse to one 20px gap.
The gaps between the paragraphs still count, two of 20px.
The outer margins above the first paragraph and below the third lie outside the span measured.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three heights add to 90px. Between each pair the margins collapse to a 20px gap, and there are two gaps, so 90 + 20 + 20 = 130px.

questions.prompt: An element has `width: 240px`, `padding: 8px 16px`, `border: 3px solid` and `box-sizing: content-box`. What is the width in px of its border box?
hints: Width covers only the content under content-box.
The horizontal padding is 16px on each side.
questions.onCorrect: Only the left and right padding affect the width. The 8px top and bottom padding affect the height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the content width only. Padding and border add to it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Under `content-box`, the border box is 240 + 16 + 16 + 3 + 3 = 278px.

questions.prompt: An element has `box-sizing: border-box`, `width: 320px`, `padding: 12px 24px` and `border: 4px solid`. What is its content width in px?
hints: Under border-box, width includes padding and border.
Subtract 24 twice and 4 twice.
questions.onCorrect: The vertical padding of 12px does not affect the width, only the height.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole border box. Padding and border come out of it.
That removes only the border. The padding comes out as well.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Under `border-box` the content is 320 - 24 - 24 - 4 - 4 = 264px.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A has margin-bottom: 28px and the block paragraph below it has margin-top: 35px. What is the gap in px?
hints: Margins that meet do not add.
Compare the two margins.
The larger one sets the gap.
questions.onCorrect: The collapse takes the larger margin, so shrinking the smaller one changes nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: Sibling margins collapse and do not add. The larger one sets the gap.
The larger margin sets the gap, and the lower paragraph has it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Adjoining vertical margins collapse to the larger, 35px.

questions.prompt: Rule 1 is `.btn.primary { color: red }` and appears first in the stylesheet. Rule 2 is `div .btn { color: blue }` and appears later. A `div` contains `<a class="btn primary">`. What colour is the link text?
hints: Score each selector before looking at where it is written.
Compare the counts from the left.
questions.onCorrect: Specificity is compared before order, so the rule written earlier can still win.

misconceptions.feedback: The later rule wins only when specificity ties. Here `.btn.primary` scores (0,2,0) against (0,1,1), so order is never consulted.
Only one value of color can apply to an element, and the cascade picks one declaration.
The order of class names in the attribute plays no part. The order that matters is the order of rules, and only after specificity ties.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: red

choices.label: red
blue
it depends on the order of the class names
purple, because both apply

questions.prompt: Work out the specificity of `.card:hover > p::first-line` as three counts in the order ids, classes, elements. Write it with commas.
hints: Count ids first, then classes and pseudo-classes, then element names and pseudo-elements.
The `>` combinator adds nothing.
questions.onCorrect: Pseudo-classes such as :hover count in the classes column, and pseudo-elements such as ::first-line count in the elements column.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The classes column holds .card and :hover, and the elements column holds p and ::first-line, so the score is (0, 2, 2).

questions.prompt: Give the specificity of `ul#menu li.active a` as three counts in the order ids, classes, elements, separated by commas.
hints: Look for `#` first, then for `.` `:` and `[ ]`, then for names of elements.
ul, li and a are three element names.
questions.onCorrect: A selector is scored by what it contains, whatever order the pieces come in.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The id is #menu, the class is .active, and the elements are ul, li and a, so the score is (1, 1, 3).

questions.prompt: A rule with the selector #title competes with a rule whose selector is ten class names chained together, such as .a.b.c.d.e.f.g.h.i.j. Both set the same property on one element. Which rule wins?
hints: Compare the columns from the left, one at a time.
Does the ids column differ?
questions.onCorrect: The columns are compared, not added, so no number of classes can outrank a single id.

misconceptions.feedback: The counts are never added into one number. They are compared from the left, and the first column that differs decides, so one id outranks any number of classes.
The scores are (1, 0, 0) and (0, 10, 0), which differ in the ids column, so the order of the rules is never consulted.

acceptedIdeas: The id selector, because the ids column is compared first
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The id selector, because the ids column is compared first

choices.label: Whichever rule is written later, because the selectors tie
The ten classes, because together they count for more than one id
The id selector, because the ids column is compared first

questions.prompt: `body { color: green; border: 1px solid; }` and a paragraph inside `body`. Which is true of the paragraph?
hints: Decide for each property whether it is one that passes down.
Text properties tend to inherit and box properties do not.
questions.onCorrect: Properties about text, such as color and font-family, inherit. Properties about boxes, such as border and margin, do not.

misconceptions.feedback: Colour is passed down to descendants, but border is not, so the paragraph is not given the body's border.
This reverses it: colour is inherited and border is not.
The text colour is inherited from body, so the paragraph's text is green.

acceptedIdeas: Its text is green but it has no border.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its text is green but it has no border.

choices.label: It has a border but black text.
Its text is green but it has no border.
It has neither.
It has a border and green text.

questions.prompt: The CSS is `body { font-size: 18px }` and `div { font-size: 24px }`. A `p` sits inside a `div` inside `body` and has no `font-size` rule of its own. What is its font size in px?
hints: Does font-size inherit?
The value comes from the closest ancestor that sets it.
The div sits between the p and the body.
questions.onCorrect: An inherited value comes from the nearest ancestor that sets it, and it is passed on again to the descendants.

misconceptions.feedback: The div sets its own value, and it is nearer to the p than the body is.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: font-size inherits, and the p takes the value from its nearest ancestor that sets one, which is the div, so 24px.

questions.prompt: The CSS is `:root { --gap: 8px } .box { --gap: 20px } .box p { margin-left: var(--gap) }`, and a `p` sits inside an element with the class `box`. What is the `p`'s `margin-left` in px?
hints: Custom properties are inherited like colour.
Which ancestor of the `p` defines `--gap` most closely?
.box redefines it.
questions.onCorrect: Redefining a custom property on one element restyles everything beneath it, which is how themes work.

misconceptions.feedback: :root sets 8px, but .box sets its own value, which is the nearer one for descendants of .box.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Custom properties inherit, and `.box` redefines `--gap` for its descendants, so `var(--gap)` inside `.box` reads 20px.

questions.prompt: Give the specificity of `:is(.a, #b) p` as three counts in the order ids, classes, elements, separated by commas. `:is()` takes the specificity of its most specific argument.
hints: Score each argument inside `:is()` and take the largest.
Then add the p.
questions.onCorrect: Wrapping a selector in `:where()` instead would contribute nothing, which is why it is used for low-specificity defaults.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The most specific argument of :is() is #b, which scores (1,0,0), and the p adds one element, giving (1, 0, 1).

questions.prompt: Give the specificity of `nav ul.menu li:first-child a[href]` as three counts in the order ids, classes, elements, separated by commas.
hints: Attribute selectors and pseudo-classes count with classes.
Count the element names last.
questions.onCorrect: Attribute selectors and structural pseudo-classes weigh the same as a class.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The classes column holds .menu, :first-child and [href], and the elements column holds nav, ul, li and a, so the score is (0, 3, 4).

questions.prompt: Rule A is `#hero p { color: red }` and Rule B is `section.intro p.lead { color: blue }`, and B is written later. A paragraph matches both. What colour is its text?
hints: Score both selectors.
Compare the ids column first.
questions.onCorrect: Order is consulted only when the scores tie, so rule B's later position counts for nothing here.

misconceptions.feedback: Order is consulted only when the scores tie. Here A scores (1, 0, 1) and B scores (0, 2, 2), so the ids column settles it before order matters.
The counts are compared column by column from the left and never added up. A has an id and B has none, so that column decides first.

acceptedIdeas: Red, because the id in rule A outranks any number of classes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Red, because the id in rule A outranks any number of classes

choices.label: Blue, because B has more classes and elements
Red, because the id in rule A outranks any number of classes
Blue, because rule B is written later

questions.prompt: Of color, font-family and border, which one is not inherited by child elements?
hints: Which of them describes a box and not text?
questions.onCorrect: Border and margin describe an element's own box, so each element has to ask for its own.
