misconceptions.feedback: font-size is about text, and text properties inherit. A child with no font-size rule of its own takes its parent's.
line-height is about the spacing of text, and properties about text inherit.

questions.prompt: A form has a label in a left column and an input in a right column on every row, and all the inputs have to start at the same distance from the left edge. Which layout mode suits that?
hints: Count how many dimensions have to line up.
Do the inputs on the second row need to sit under the inputs on the first?

acceptedIdeas: Grid, because two columns have to line up across every row
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Grid, because two columns have to line up across every row

questions.onCorrect: Columns that stay the same width on every row need two dimensions to line up, and that is what grid is for.

choices.label: Flexbox, because each row is a single line of items
Grid, because two columns have to line up across every row
Flexbox, because it is the more flexible of the two modes

misconceptions.feedback: Each row can be a flex line, but separate flex lines are arranged on their own and do not line up with each other.
How flexible a mode is does not decide it. The test is how many dimensions have to line up.

questions.prompt: Which of these values are falsy: `-1`, `'false'`, `{}`, `undefined`, `0n` and `' '`, a string holding one space?
hints: Recall the short list of falsy values. Everything else is truthy.
A string is falsy only when it is empty.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `undefined` and `0n`

questions.onCorrect: Only the eight listed values are falsy. Of these six, `undefined` and `0n` are on the list and the other four are truthy.

choices.label: `-1`, `{}` and `undefined`
`undefined`, `0n` and `' '`
`'false'` and `undefined`
`undefined` and `0n`

misconceptions.feedback: A negative number is truthy and so is an empty object. Among numeric values only 0, -0, 0n and NaN are falsy, and no object is.
A string holding a space is not the empty string, so it is truthy.
The string 'false' is non-empty, and every non-empty string is truthy whatever it says.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(undefined == false, undefined === undefined)` print?
hints: Loose equality gives undefined only one other value to equal.
Strict equality compares the type and the value, and a value always matches itself.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: false true

questions.onCorrect: undefined is loosely equal only to null and to itself, so it does not equal false, and a value is always strictly equal to itself.

misconceptions.feedback: false does turn into 0 in some loose comparisons, but undefined is loosely equal only to null and to itself.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(0.3 - 0.1 === 0.2)` print?
hints: Decimal tenths are stored with a tiny error.
Compare the stored difference with the stored 0.2.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: false

questions.onCorrect: The subtraction gives 0.19999999999999998, not the stored 0.2, so the comparison fails. To compare such results, test whether the difference is smaller than a small tolerance.

questions.prompt: What does `console.log(null == false, [] == '')` print?
hints: null is loosely equal only to undefined and to itself.
An empty array becomes the empty string when it is compared with a string.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: false true

questions.onCorrect: null is not loosely equal to false, and an empty array becomes the empty string, so the second comparison holds.

questions.prompt: Which of these comparisons prints true?
hints: Which of these is built from fractions that are sums of powers of two?
Halves, quarters and eighths are stored exactly.
questions.onCorrect: Eighths and halves are sums of powers of two, so they are stored exactly. The rounding problem belongs to fractions such as 0.1, which have no exact binary form.

misconceptions.feedback: 0.1 * 3 comes to 0.30000000000000004, a hair above the stored 0.3, because 0.1 has no exact binary form.
0.6 + 0.3 comes to 0.8999999999999999, a hair below the stored 0.9.
0.1 + 0.7 comes to 0.7999999999999999, a hair below the stored 0.8.

questions.prompt:
`let n = 0;`
`const get = () => n * 2;`
`n = 5;`
`console.log(get());`
What does this print?
hints: Did the function take a copy of n, or does it use n itself?
Check when n changes compared with when get is called.
get is called after n has changed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The function keeps the variable n, not a copy of its value at the time the function was made, so it sees the later 5 and doubles it to 10.

questions.onCorrect: A closure keeps the variable, so changes made after it was created are visible to it.

misconceptions.feedback: The function does not hold a copy of the value 0. It reads the variable n each time it is called.
That is the value of n. The function doubles it.

questions.prompt:
`const a = [3, 1, 2];`
`const b = [...a].sort();`
`console.log(a[0] + b[0]);`
What does this print?
hints: Which array does sort reorder here?
`[...a]` is a new array.
a itself is never changed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The spread made a new array, and sort reordered only that copy. So a[0] is still 3 and b[0] is 1, and 3 + 1 is 4.

questions.onCorrect: Copying first, as in `[...a].sort()` or `a.toSorted()`, keeps the original order.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats a as sorted too, giving 1 + 1. The sort ran on the copy, so a[0] is still 3.
That treats b as unsorted, giving 3 + 3. The sort reordered the copy, so b[0] is 1.

questions.prompt:
`const team = { size: 3 };`
`const copy = team;`
`copy.size = copy.size * 2;`
`console.log(team.size);`
What does this print?
hints: Does `copy = team` make a second object?
Both names point at the same object.
Doubling copy.size changes that object.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `copy = team` copies the reference, so both names refer to one object. The assignment doubles its size from 3 to 6, and team.size reads the same object.

questions.onCorrect: To get an independent object, copy it with `{...team}` for a flat object.

misconceptions.feedback: copy is not a separate object. It is another name for team's object, so the doubled size shows through team.

questions.prompt:
`setTimeout(() => console.log('a'), 50);`
`setTimeout(() => console.log('b'), 10);`
`setTimeout(() => console.log('c'), 30);`
`console.log('d');`
What is printed, in order? Write the four letters with spaces.
hints: The script runs to the end before any timer callback.
The timers run in the order in which they become due.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: d b c a

questions.onCorrect: The task queue orders timers by when they become due, not by the order they were written.

questions.prompt: The first microtask has printed m1 and has queued a second microtask, and the timer's task is still waiting. What does the event loop run next?
hints: The script comes first, then the microtasks.
A microtask queued by a microtask is still a microtask.

acceptedIdeas: The second microtask, which prints m2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The second microtask, which prints m2

questions.onCorrect: The microtask queue drains fully, including anything queued while it drains, before the next task runs.

choices.label: The second microtask, which prints m2
The timer's task, which prints t1
Nothing, until a new event arrives

misconceptions.feedback: The loop empties the microtask queue completely before it takes a task, and the second microtask is in that queue.
The queues still hold callbacks, and the loop keeps taking from them until both are empty.

questions.prompt: A button sits in div#inner, which sits in div#outer. Each of the three has a bubbling click listener that logs its id (button, inner, outer), and div#inner also has a capture click listener that logs inner-capture. The button is clicked. What is logged, in order? Write the four ids with spaces.
hints: Capture listeners run on the way down.
Bubbling listeners run on the way up, starting with the button.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: inner-capture button inner outer

questions.onCorrect: The capture and bubble phases give each ancestor two chances to hear the event.

questions.prompt: A button sits in `div#inner`, which sits in `div#outer`. Each of the three has a bubbling click listener that logs its id (`button`, `inner`, `outer`), and the button's listener also calls `event.stopPropagation()`. The button is clicked. What is logged, in order?
hints: What does stopPropagation stop?
The button's own listener still runs.

acceptedIdeas: button only, because the event goes no further than the button
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: button only, because the event goes no further than the button

questions.onCorrect: stopPropagation ends the journey to further elements, whereas preventDefault cancels the browser's default action, and neither does the other's job.

choices.label: inner, outer, because the call skips the button's own listener
button, inner, outer, because the listeners on the ancestors still run
button only, because the event goes no further than the button

misconceptions.feedback: The listener that calls stopPropagation still finishes its own work. It is the elements further along that are skipped.
stopPropagation ends the journey, so the ancestors never hear the click.

questions.prompt: A single click listener is on `div#menu`. Inside it is `Home`, and the user clicks the word Home. What is `event.target.tagName`?
hints: target is the element where the event started.
Which element is deepest at the point of the click?

acceptedIdeas: B, the deepest element at the point of the click
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: B, the deepest element at the point of the click

questions.onCorrect: target is where the click happened and currentTarget is where the listener is, and with delegation they differ.

choices.label: DIV, the element that holds the listener
B, the deepest element at the point of the click
A, the link the user thinks they clicked

misconceptions.feedback: `DIV` is `event.currentTarget`, the element the listener is attached to. The target is the element where the click began.
The a element contains the b, but the click landed on the b, which is the deepest element at that point.

questions.prompt: An `ol` has a click listener that logs `event.target.tagName` and `event.currentTarget.tagName`, separated by a space. Each `li` contains an `em`. The user clicks the text inside an `em`. What is logged?
hints: Which element is deepest at the point of the click?
The listener is attached to the ol.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: EM OL

questions.onCorrect: Delegating code often needs `target.closest('li')` to find the item when the click lands on something inside it.

questions.prompt:
`console.log(JSON.parse('{"a":[1,2,{"b":[7,8,9]}]}').a[2].b[1]);`
What is printed?
hints: Parse first, then follow the property names and the indexes.
a is an array, and index 2 is its third item.
The item at index 2 is an object whose b is another array.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `parse` turns the text into an object. `a[2]` is the third item of the array, an object, and its `b[1]` is the second item of the array [7, 8, 9], which is 8.

questions.onCorrect: parse is the inverse of stringify for values that JSON can express.

misconceptions.feedback: Indexes start at 0, so b[0] is 7. The index here is 1.
That is b[2]. The index here is 1, the second item.
a[1] would be 2. Follow a[2] first, then b[1].

questions.prompt:
`console.log(typeof JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ n: NaN })).n);`
What is printed?
hints: What does stringify write for NaN?
Then ask what typeof says about that value.

acceptedIdeas: object, because stringify writes NaN as null, and typeof null is 'object'
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: object, because stringify writes NaN as null, and typeof null is 'object'

questions.onCorrect: NaN becomes null in the text, and typeof null is 'object', so the round trip changes both the value and its type.

choices.label: object, because stringify writes NaN as null, and typeof null is 'object'
number, because NaN survives the round trip
undefined, because stringify leaves out values it cannot express

misconceptions.feedback: JSON has no NaN. stringify writes it as null, so parse gives back null and not a number.
An undefined property or a function is left out of an object, but NaN is written as null, so the property remains.

questions.prompt: A server replies with status 200 and the body `not json at all`, and the code awaits `res.json()`. What happens?
hints: Which promise does the parsing: the one from fetch, or the one from json()?
JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError for text that is not JSON.

acceptedIdeas: `res.json()` rejects with a SyntaxError, because the text is not valid JSON
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: `res.json()` rejects with a SyntaxError, because the text is not valid JSON

questions.onCorrect: The status was fine, but the body was not JSON, so the promise from res.json() rejects. A try and catch around the await handles it.

choices.label: The fetch promise rejects, because the body is invalid
`res.json()` rejects with a SyntaxError, because the text is not valid JSON
`res.json()` resolves with the text unchanged

misconceptions.feedback: The fetch promise settled when the headers arrived, long before the body was read. Reading the body is a later step with its own promise.
json() does not hand back text. It parses, and text that is not JSON makes its promise reject.

questions.prompt:
`console.log(Number(localStorage.getItem('never-set')));`
What is printed?
hints: What does getItem return for a key that was never stored?
What does null become when it is converted to a number?

acceptedIdeas: 0, because getItem returns null and Number(null) is 0
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0, because getItem returns null and Number(null) is 0

questions.onCorrect: A missing key gives null, and Number turns null into 0, so a missing setting can look like a stored zero. Code that reads a stored number checks for null first.

choices.label: 0, because getItem returns null and Number(null) is 0
NaN, because nothing was stored
null, because Number leaves null as it is

misconceptions.feedback: NaN would come from a string such as 'abc'. getItem gives null for a key that was never stored, and null converts to 0.
Number always returns a number. It converts null to 0.

questions.prompt: A page greets a visitor with `el.innerHTML = 'Hello ' + name`, where `name` comes from the address bar. What is the safest minimal fix?
hints: The aim is that the text is never parsed as markup.
Which property inserts text as text?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use `el.textContent` in place of `el.innerHTML`

questions.onCorrect: Avoiding the parser removes the whole class of problem, where filtering has to catch every trick.

choices.label: Escape only the `<` character before inserting it
Use `el.textContent` in place of `el.innerHTML`
Remove the word script from the name
Add a Content-Security-Policy header and keep innerHTML

misconceptions.feedback: Escaping one character is a hand-made filter, and each trick it misses still works.
Removing one word leaves other ways to run code, such as an event-handler attribute on an image.
A Content-Security-Policy is a second line of defence, but it leaves the parser reading untrusted markup. The minimal fix removes that step.

questions.prompt:
`sessionStorage.setItem('count', 0);`
`console.log(sessionStorage.getItem('count') ? 'set' : 'empty');`
What is printed?
hints: What does getItem return after storing 0?
Is a non-empty string truthy?

acceptedIdeas: set, because the stored text '0' is a non-empty string
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: set, because the stored text '0' is a non-empty string

questions.onCorrect: A stored number has to be converted back with `Number(...)` before it is tested.

choices.label: empty, because the value that was stored is 0
set, because the stored text '0' is a non-empty string
An error, because 0 cannot be stored

misconceptions.feedback: Storage keeps strings, so the stored value is the text '0'. Any non-empty string counts as true in a condition, whatever it says.
setItem accepts any value and converts it to text, so storing 0 is allowed and stores the string '0'.

flashcards.front: Which part of a URL stays in the browser and is not sent in the request?
flashcards.back: The fragment, after the #, names a place in the finished page, so only the browser needs it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The fragment, after the #, names a place in the finished page, so only the browser needs it.

flashcards.front: A response has a status beginning with 5. Whose side has the fault?
flashcards.back: The server's: the request reached it and it failed to carry the request out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The server's: the request reached it and it failed to carry the request out.

flashcards.front: Which element does the parser insert between table and tr?
flashcards.back: The tree gains a tbody, because the parsing rules require rows to sit inside a table section.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The tree gains a tbody, because the parsing rules require rows to sit inside a table section.

flashcards.front: Which element, a or button, is right for a control that does something on the page and goes nowhere?
flashcards.back: A button, because a link goes somewhere and a button does something, and the button carries keyboard activation with it.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A button, because a link goes somewhere and a button does something, and the button carries keyboard activation with it.

flashcards.front: What does `alt=""` tell assistive technology?
flashcards.back: That the image is decoration, so it is skipped and not announced.

flashcards.front: Which attribute on a label names the input it belongs to, by matching the input's id?
flashcards.back: The for attribute, which makes the label's text part of the input's name.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The for attribute, which makes the label's text part of the input's name.

flashcards.front: Under `box-sizing: border-box`, what does `width: 200px` cover?
flashcards.back: Content, padding and border together, so the content shrinks as padding and border grow.

flashcards.front: Block siblings have margins of 30px and 20px where they meet. What is the gap in px?
flashcards.back: 30, because adjoining vertical margins collapse to the larger of the two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30, because adjoining vertical margins collapse to the larger of the two.

flashcards.front: Which layer of the box lies outside the border?
flashcards.back: The margin, which reserves space around an element and is not part of its size.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The margin, which reserves space around an element and is not part of its size.

flashcards.front: Which wins, one id selector or ten class selectors, when both set the same property?
flashcards.back: The id selector, because the columns are compared from the left and not added together.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The id selector, because the columns are compared from the left and not added together.

flashcards.front: What is the specificity of `.btn.primary`, as three counts?
flashcards.back: (0, 2, 0): no ids, two classes, no elements.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: (0, 2, 0): no ids, two classes, no elements.

flashcards.front: Does border pass from a parent to its children?
flashcards.back: No: border describes the element's own box, and only some properties, such as color, inherit.

flashcards.front: What does flex-grow share out?
flashcards.back: Only the free space left after every item takes its basis, in proportion to the grow factors.

flashcards.front: A 600px flex row has three items of basis 100px and flex-grow 1, 2 and 3. How wide in px is the second?
flashcards.back: The 300px of free space gives each grow unit 50px, so the second is 100 + 100 = 200px.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 300px of free space gives each grow unit 50px, so the second is 100 + 100 = 200px.

flashcards.front: In a grid of columns 1fr 2fr 100px, what do the fr units share?
flashcards.back: What remains after the fixed track and the gaps, and not the whole container.

flashcards.front: What does 5vw come to on a 1200px-wide viewport, in px?
flashcards.back: One vw is 1% of the viewport width, so 5vw is 60px.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One vw is 1% of the viewport width, so 5vw is 60px.

flashcards.front: Which meta tag lets a mobile browser lay a page out at the device's width?
flashcards.back: The viewport meta tag, `name="viewport"` with `width=device-width`, because without it the page is laid out at a wide virtual width and shrunk.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The viewport meta tag, name="viewport" with width=device-width, because without it the page is laid out at a wide virtual width and shrunk.

flashcards.front: Why are min-width queries written from smallest to largest?
flashcards.back: Later rules of equal specificity win, so each larger breakpoint can override the one before it.

flashcards.front: Give the string that typeof null evaluates to.
flashcards.back: The string 'object', a quirk kept from the first version of the language.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The string 'object', a quirk kept from the first version of the language.

flashcards.front: Is the string '0' truthy or falsy?
flashcards.back: Truthy, because every non-empty string is truthy, whatever it contains.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Truthy, because every non-empty string is truthy, whatever it contains.

flashcards.front: Give the exact value that 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to in JavaScript.
flashcards.back: 0.30000000000000004, because 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be stored exactly in binary.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0.30000000000000004, because 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be stored exactly in binary.

flashcards.front: Does a closure copy the value of a variable, or keep the variable itself?
flashcards.back: It keeps the variable itself, so later changes to it are visible inside the closure.

flashcards.front: Name the value that a var holds before the line that assigns it has run.
flashcards.back: undefined: the declaration is hoisted and the assignment is not.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: undefined: the declaration is hoisted and the assignment is not.

flashcards.front: What does a let loop head give each iteration?
flashcards.back: A fresh copy of the loop variable, which is why callbacks made in the loop keep their own value.

flashcards.front: Does const make an object unchangeable?
flashcards.back: No: const stops the name being reassigned, and the object it points at can still be changed.

flashcards.front: Does sort change its array in place?
flashcards.back: Yes, it reorders the array it is called on and returns that same array.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, it reorders the array it is called on and returns that same array.

flashcards.front: Give the number of levels of an object that a spread copy duplicates.
flashcards.back: One, the top level: nested objects stay shared with the original.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One, the top level: nested objects stay shared with the original.

flashcards.front: Which queue holds promise callbacks, the task queue or the microtask queue?
flashcards.back: The microtask queue, which is emptied completely before the next task is taken.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The microtask queue, which is emptied completely before the next task is taken.

flashcards.front: Does await block the whole program?
flashcards.back: No: it suspends only the async function, and the rest of the program carries on.

flashcards.front: Which runs first, a promise callback or a zero-delay timer callback queued by the same script?
flashcards.back: The promise callback, because microtasks run before the next task.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The promise callback, because microtasks run before the next task.

flashcards.front: Which is bigger for an element with whitespace between its tags, `children.length` or `childNodes.length`?
flashcards.back: `childNodes`, because it counts the whitespace text nodes as well as the elements.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: childNodes, because it counts the whitespace text nodes as well as the elements.

flashcards.front: Does `stopPropagation` cancel a link's default action?
flashcards.back: No: it only stops the event travelling to other elements, and `preventDefault` is what cancels the default action.

flashcards.front: In a delegated listener, which property holds the element that was actually clicked?
flashcards.back: `event.target`, while `currentTarget` is the element the listener is attached to.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: event.target, while currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to.

flashcards.front: When does the promise from fetch reject?
flashcards.back: Only when the request itself fails, as when the host cannot be reached, and never because of a 404 or 500.

flashcards.front: Give the value that JSON.stringify writes for undefined inside an array.
flashcards.back: They become null inside an array, since the array keeps its positions.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They become null inside an array, since the array keeps its positions.

flashcards.front: Name the three parts of a URL that together make up its origin.
flashcards.back: The scheme, host and port.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The scheme, the host and the port.

flashcards.front: What type does `localStorage.getItem` always return, apart from `null`?
flashcards.back: A string, whatever type was stored, so numbers and booleans need converting when read.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A string, whatever type was stored, so numbers and booleans need converting when read.

flashcards.front: Which property inserts untrusted text safely, `textContent` or `innerHTML`?
flashcards.back: `textContent`, because it inserts the text without parsing it as markup.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: textContent, because it inserts the text without parsing it as markup.

flashcards.front: Why is an HttpOnly cookie safer for a session token than `localStorage`?
flashcards.back: Page scripts cannot read an HttpOnly cookie, so a script injected into the page cannot steal the token.

flashcards.front: What is the minimum contrast ratio for WCAG AA for normal-size text?
flashcards.back: 4.5 to 1, with 3 to 1 allowed for large text.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4.5 to 1, with 3 to 1 allowed for large text.

flashcards.front: Which Core Web Vital measures loading, and what does it time?
flashcards.back: Largest Contentful Paint, which times how long the largest element takes to appear.

flashcards.front: Name the three Core Web Vitals by their abbreviations, loading first.
flashcards.back: LCP, INP, CLS: loading, responsiveness and visual stability, in that order.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness and CLS for visual stability.
